question_text: Concerning the relation between performance and stress, which of the following statement(s) is (are) correct?
option_a: A moderate level of stress may improve performance.
option_b: A student will learn faster and better under severe stress.
option_c: Domestic stress will not affect the pilot's performance because he is able to leave this type of stress on the ground.
option_d: A well trained pilot is able to eleminate any kind of stress completely when he is scheduled to fly.
explanation: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, the relationship between stress (arousal) and performance is an inverted U-curve. A moderate level of stress optimizes arousal and improves performance, whereas too little stress leads to boredom and too much stress leads to cognitive overload.

question_text: Stress is a frequent aspect of the pilot's job. Under which of the following circumstances does it occur?1. Stress occurs whenever the pilot must revise his plan of action and does not immediately have a solution2. Stress occurs with unexperienced pilots when the situational demands exceed their individual capabilities3. Stress occurs if a pilot is convinced that he will not be able to find a solution for the problem he just is confronted with
option_a: 1, 2 and 3 are correct
explanation: Stress is triggered by a perceived imbalance between environmental demands and personal capabilities. This occurs when a pilot must revise a plan without an immediate solution, when demands exceed capabilities, or when the pilot believes no solution is available.

question_text: Divided attention is the ability :1. to execute several mental activities at almost the same time (i.e. when switching attention from outside the aircraft to the airspeed indicator on the instrument panel)2. to monitor the progress of a motor programme (i.e. flying or taxiing the airplane) on a relatively subconscious level, while making a radio call at the same time (requiring a rather conscious level)3 .to select information and check if it is relevant to the task in hand. At the same time no other operation can be performed.4. to delegate tasks to the copilot while concentrating on the procedures
option_a: 1 and 2 are correct, 3 and 4 are false
option_c: 1 and 3 are correct, 2 and 4 are false
explanation: Divided attention is the capability to manage multiple tasks concurrently or sequentially by rapidly switching focus or by executing automated motor tasks subconsciously while consciously focusing on another task.

question_text: The physiology of stress is now well known:
option_a: stress promotes an increase in physical strength rather than promoting mental oerformance
option_b: the only stress hormone is adrenaline
option_c: stress develops in 2 stages: sublimation of performance and then acceleration of heart rate and increase in vision
option_d: stress slows down the production of sugar by the organism and thereby slows down the heart rate
explanation: The physiological stress response (the fight-or-flight response) prepares the body for immediate physical action by releasing adrenaline, which increases heart rate, dilates bronchioles, and redirects blood flow to large muscles, prioritizing physical strength over complex cognitive processing.

question_text: An overstressed pilot may show the following symptoms:1. mental blocks, confusion and channelized attention2. resignation, frustration, rage3. deterioration in motor coordination4. high pitch voice and fast speaking
option_a: 1, 2, 3 and 4 are correct
option_c: 1 and 2 are correct, 3 and 4 are false
explanation: Excessive stress leads to cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and physiological symptoms. These include mental blocks and channelized attention, frustration or resignation, loss of motor coordination, and a high-pitched voice with rapid speech.

question_text: In the initial phase of flight training the relationship between confidence and expertise can be described as:
option_a: the pilot is competent enough to fly the aircraft at this stage, but does neither have a great deal of confidence in his/her abilities nor in the whole system
option_b: the pilot is sufficiently competent to fly and knows at this stage what he can and cannot do
option_c: during this learning stage, the pilot is very near to achieving full potential knowledge of the machine
option_d: the pilot has a sphere of expertise wich is reduced to daily use of his skills
explanation: Early in flight training, a student's confidence lags behind their actual basic competence because they are highly aware of their limitations and have not yet built trust in their own skills or the aviation system.

question_text: A pilot is skilled when he :-1 : trains or practises regularly-2 : knows how to manage himself/herself-3 : possesses all the knowledge associated with his aircraft-4 : knows how to keep resources in reserve for coping with the unexpected
explanation: Skill development relies on regular practice and training and self-management. Furthermore, a skilled pilot knows how to conserve mental and physical resources as reserves to handle unexpected events. Simply possessing theoretical knowledge without application does not define a skilled pilot.

question_text: The rate of accidents in commercial aviation (excluding sabotage and acts of terrorism) :
option_a: is approximatively 1 accident per million airport movements
option_b: has improved considerably over the last fifteen years
option_c: is a long way short of the safety level of road transport
option_d: represents about fifty accidents around the world every year
explanation: Statistical records for modern commercial jet aviation show that the accident rate is extremely low, hovering at approximately one major hull-loss accident per one million flight cycles (airport movements).

question_text: As a cause of accidents, the human factor
option_a: is cited in approximately 70 - 80 % of aviation accidents
option_b: has increased considerably since 1980 - the percentage of accident in which this factor has been involved has more than tripled since this date
option_c: which is cited in current statistics, applies to the flight crew and ATC only
option_d: plays a negligible role in commercial aviation accidents. It is much more important in general aviation
explanation: Numerous studies and accident investigations consistently show that human error (the human factor) is a primary or contributing cause in approximately 70% to 80% of all aviation accidents.

question_text: What airplane equipment marked a subtantial decrease in hull loss rates in the eighties?
option_a: GPWS
explanation: The introduction of the Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) in the late 1970s and 1980s significantly reduced the occurrence of Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT) accidents, resulting in a dramatic drop in commercial hull loss rates.

question_text: In civil air transport, linear accelerations (Gx):- 1 : do not exist- 2 : have slight physiological consequences- 3 : may, in the case of pull-out, lead to loss of consciousness- 4 : cause sensory illusions on the pitch axis
explanation: Linear accelerations along the chest-to-back axis (Gx) are experienced during takeoff and braking in civil aviation; they have minor physiological effects but can trigger somatogravic illusions, leading the pilot to falsely perceive a pitch change. Pull-out maneuvers involve vertical accelerations (Gz), not linear Gx.

question_text: Thinking on human reliability is changing.
option_a: Human errors are now considered as being inherent to the cognitive function of human and are generally inescapable
option_b: Human errors can be avoided. All it takes is to be vigilant and to extend one's knowledge
option_c: The individual view of safety has gradually replaced the systemic view of safety
option_d: It is thought that it will be possible to eliminate errors in the near future
explanation: Modern human factors theory views error as a natural, inevitable consequence of human cognitive processing under limits. Safety systems are therefore designed to be error-tolerant rather than expecting humans to perform error-free.

question_text: Between which components is an interface mismatch causing an error of interpretation by using an old three-point altimeter?
option_a: Liveware - Hardware
explanation: In the SHELL model, the interface between the human (Liveware) and the physical equipment or controls (Hardware) is represented as L-H. Misinterpreting a mechanical three-point altimeter is a Liveware-Hardware mismatch.

question_text: Between which components is an interface mismatch responsible for deficiencies in conceptual aspects of warning systems?
option_a: Liveware - Software
explanation: Software in the SHELL model refers to non-physical aspects like procedures, symbology, conceptual display rules, and warning logic. Deficiencies in the design of warning system concepts are a Liveware-Software mismatch.

question_text: Between which components is an interface mismatch causing disturbance of the biological rhythm, thus leading to reduced human peformance?
option_a: Liveware - Environment
explanation: The Environment (E) in the SHELL model represents the physical surroundings, including timezone changes, cabin temperature, noise, and light. Jet lag and sleep schedule disruption are mismatches between Liveware and the Environment.

question_text: The errors resulting from an irrational indexing system in an operations manual are related to an interface mismatch between
option_a: Liveware - Software
explanation: Under the SHELL model, manuals, documents, maps, and procedures represent Software (S). An irrational or confusing layout in an operations manual constitutes a Liveware-Software mismatch.

question_text: Man possesses a system for maintaining his internal equilibrium in the face of variations brought about by external stimulations.This internal equilibrium is called :
option_a: Homeostasis
explanation: Homeostasis is the physiological process by which living organisms maintain a stable internal environment (such as body temperature, blood pH, and fluid balance) despite changes in external conditions.

question_text: The earth's atmosphere consists of different gases in various concentration. Match the following:1 nitrogen A 0,03%2 oxygen B 0,92%3 carbon dioxide C 20.95%4 rare gas D 78,10%
explanation: The dry atmosphere near sea level is composed of approximately 78.10% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.03% carbon dioxide, and 0.92% rare gases (mostly argon).

question_text: Gases of physiological importance to man are:
option_a: oxygen and carbon dioxide
explanation: Oxygen (needed for metabolic cellular respiration) and carbon dioxide (which regulates the blood's pH level and drives the breathing trigger) are the two gases of primary physiological importance to human life.

question_text: The volume percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere is 21% which
option_a: is constant for all altitudes conventional airplanes can reach
option_d: is dependent on the present air pressure
explanation: Due to atmospheric mixing, the relative volume percentage of gases (21% oxygen and 78% nitrogen) remains constant up to approximately 300,000 feet. Only the total pressure and density decrease with altitude.

question_text: The following applies for the physical properties of gases:
option_a: at sea-level a gas has 1/3 of the volume it would have at 27000 ft
option_b: at an altitude of 18 000 ft a gas volume is three times as large as it would be at sea-level
option_c: a water vapor saturated gas at 34 000 ft has 6 times its volume as it would have at sea- level
option_d: at an altitute of 63 000 ft water will boil at temperature of 65°C
explanation: According to Boyle's law (volume is inversely proportional to pressure), since the atmospheric pressure at 27,000 feet is approximately 1/3 of that at sea level, a gas volume will expand to 3 times its size at 27,000 feet compared to sea level.

question_text: The percentage of oxygen in the air at an altitude of approximately 34 000 ft is :
explanation: Throughout the homosphere, the relative proportion of gases remains constant; therefore, the concentration of oxygen remains at 21% even at 34,000 feet.

question_text: The atmospheric gas pressure
option_a: drops faster at lower altitudes in comparison to the same altitude changes at higher altitudes
option_d: decreases slower at lower altitudes compared with higher levels and equivalent altitude changes
explanation: Because air is compressible, the density and pressure of the atmosphere drop exponentially rather than linearly. The pressure drops much faster per unit of altitude change in the denser air near the surface than at higher altitudes.

question_text: A certain amount of water vapor saturated air (i.e. intestinal gases) is transported from sea-level up to 34 000 ft. In the same amount of dry air, the volume of this gas is :
option_a: larger
explanation: Saturated air contains water vapor, which exerts its own vapor pressure. As altitude increases, the water vapor maintains a constant vapor pressure, causing the saturated gas to expand to a larger volume than dry air would under the same pressure drop.

question_text: You can survive at any altitude, provided that
option_a: enough oxygen, pressure and heat is available
option_b: 21% oxygen is available in the air you breath in
option_c: pressure respiration is guaranteed for that altitude
option_d: the temperature in the cabin does not drop below 10"" C
explanation: Human survival requires a combination of adequate partial pressure of oxygen to prevent hypoxia, sufficient total barometric pressure to prevent body fluids from boiling, and temperature control to prevent exposure.

question_text: Fatigue and permanent concentration
option_a: lower the tolerance to hypoxia
option_c: do not affect hypoxia at all
option_d: will increase the tolerance to hypoxia when flying below 15 000 feet
explanation: Physiological stressors such as fatigue, physical exhaustion, and heavy mental workload increase the body's metabolic demand and lower its baseline tolerance to oxygen deprivation, accelerating the onset of hypoxia.

question_text: The atmosphere contains the following gases:
option_a: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0,03% carbon dioxide, rest: rare gases
option_b: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% carbon monoxide, rest: rare gases
option_c: 78% helium, 21% oxygen, 1% carbon monoxide, rest: rare gases
option_d: 78% helium, 21% oxygen, 0,03% carbon dioxide, rest: rare gases
explanation: By volume, dry air in the Earth's lower atmosphere contains approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.03% carbon dioxide, and about 1% rare gases.

question_text: An increase in the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood leads to:
option_a: shortness of breath
option_b: a decrease of acidity in the blood
option_c: a reduction of red blood cells
explanation: High levels of carbon dioxide in the blood (hypercapnia) lower blood pH. This acidity stimulates the respiratory center in the brain stem, triggering an increase in depth and rate of breathing, which is perceived as shortness of breath.

question_text: The total pressure of a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the gases which compose the mixture corresponds to:
option_a: Dalton´s law
explanation: Dalton's law of partial pressures states that the total pressure exerted by a mixture of non-reactive gases is equal to the sum of the individual partial pressures that each gas would exert if it were alone in the volume.

question_text: The chemical composition of the earth´s atmosphere (I C A O standard atmosphere) is
option_a: 78 % nitrogen, 21 % oxygen, 0,9 % argon, 0,03 % carbon dioxide
explanation: The ICAO standard atmospheric gas composition by volume consists of 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon, and 0.03% carbon dioxide.

question_text: According to the I.C.A.O. standard atmosphere, the temperature lapse rate of the troposphere is approximately
option_a: - 2 °C every 1000 feet
explanation: The ICAO standard atmosphere defines a uniform temperature lapse rate of 1.98°C (commonly rounded to 2°C) decrease per 1000 feet of altitude increase within the troposphere, up to the tropopause.

question_text: The barometric pressure has dropped to 1/2 of the pressure at sea level at
option_a: 18 000 feet
explanation: Due to the exponential decrease of pressure with altitude, standard atmospheric pressure (1013.25 hPa) drops by half (to approximately 500 hPa) at an altitude of 18,000 feet.

question_text: The atmospheric pressure at 18,000 feet altitude is half the atmospheric pressure at sea level.In accordance with this statement,
option_a: the partial oxygen pressure at that altitude will also drop to 1/2 of the pressure of oxygen at sea level
option_b: the oxygen saturation of the blood at that altitude will drop by 50 % too
option_c: the oxygen percentage of the air at that altitude will drop by one half also
option_d: the partial oxygen pressure at that altitude will be doubled
explanation: According to Dalton's law, since the total atmospheric pressure at 18,000 feet is half of its sea-level value and the percentage of oxygen remains constant (21%), the partial pressure of oxygen must also drop to exactly half of its sea-level value.

question_text: The volume percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere at 30.000 feet remains at 21 %, but the partial pressure of oxygen :
option_a: decreases with decreasing barometric pressure
explanation: The partial pressure of a gas is the product of its fraction and the total pressure. Since the barometric pressure decreases with altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen decreases correspondingly, even though its volume percentage remains at 21%.

question_text: Which data compose the ICAO standard atmosphere ?1. Density2. Pressure3. Temperature4. Humidity
explanation: The ICAO standard atmosphere is a mathematical model of dry air. It is defined by standard profiles of temperature, pressure, and density, excluding humidity.

question_text: Boyle's law is directly applicable in case of:
option_a: the expansion of trapped gasses in the human body with increasing altitude
option_b: the occurance of decompression sickness at high altitude
option_c: the occurance of hypoxia with increasing altitude
explanation: Boyle's law states that at a constant temperature, gas volume is inversely proportional to pressure. As an aircraft climbs and ambient pressure drops, gases trapped in the middle ear, sinuses, and intestines expand, which can cause pain.

question_text: Dalton's law explains the occurance of :
option_a: altitude hypoxia
explanation: Dalton's law relates total pressure to the sum of partial pressures. At altitude, the drop in total atmospheric pressure reduces the partial pressure of oxygen in the lungs, reducing oxygen transfer to the blood and causing hypoxia.

question_text: Henry's Law explains the occurence of:
option_a: decompression sickness
explanation: Henry's law states that the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to the partial pressure of that gas. When ambient pressure drops rapidly, dissolved nitrogen in body tissues comes out of solution as bubbles, causing decompression sickness.

question_text: Oxygen, combined with hemoglobin in blood is transported by
option_a: red blood cells
explanation: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) contain the iron-rich protein hemoglobin, which chemically binds with oxygen in the lungs and transports it to the body's tissues.

question_text: The respiratory process consists mainly of
option_a: the diffusion of oxygen through the respiratory membranes into the blood, transportation to the cells, diffusion into the cells and elimination of carbon dioxide from the body
option_b: the transportation of oxygen to the cell and the elimination of carbon monoxide
option_c: the transportation of oxygen to the cell and the elimination of nitrogen
option_d: the transportation of carbon dioxide to the cell and elimination of oxygen
explanation: Respiration involves ventilation, external respiration (diffusion of oxygen across alveolar membranes into the blood), transport by the circulatory system, internal respiration, and removal of carbon dioxide.

question_text: Inhaling carbon monoxide can be extremely dangerous during flying. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?
option_a: Carbon monoxide is odourless and cannot be smelled.
option_b: Carbon monoxide increases the oxygen saturation in the blood.
option_c: With increasing altitude the negative effects of carbon monoxide poisoning will be compensated.
option_d: Small amounts of carbon monoxide are harmless.
explanation: Carbon monoxide is a highly toxic, colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas. This makes it impossible to detect by human senses alone, creating a severe hazard if it leaks into the cabin.

question_text: Carbon monoxide poisoning
option_a: is more likely to occur in aeroplanes where the cabin heat is technically supplied by coating the exhaust
option_b: is more likely to occur in aeroplanes with twin-engines because of high engine efficiency
explanation: Many light aircraft heat the cabin by ducting fresh air over a metal shroud around the engine exhaust tailpipe. Any cracks or corrosion in the exhaust pipe will allow exhaust gases containing carbon monoxide to enter the cabin.

question_text: In the following list you will find several symptoms listed for hypoxia and carbon monoxide poisoning. Please mark those referring to carbon monoxide poisoning.
option_a: Headache, increasing nausea, dizziness.
option_b: High levels of arousal, increased error proneness, lack of accuracy.
option_d: Muscular spasms, mental confusion, impairment of hearing.
explanation: While hypoxia and CO poisoning share symptoms like cognitive impairment, classic early symptoms of CO poisoning include throbbing headaches, increasing nausea, lethargy, and dizziness due to cellular hypoxia and systemic toxicity.

question_text: A pilot, climbing in a non-pressurised aircraft and without using supplemental oxygen will pass the ""critical threshold"" at approximately:
explanation: In aviation physiology, the critical threshold (where severe hypoxia causes loss of function or consciousness within a short time) is reached at approximately 20,000 to 22,000 feet for an unacclimatized pilot.

question_text: Breathing 100% will lift the pilot's physiological safe altitude to approximately:
explanation: Inhaling 100% oxygen compensates for the lower atmospheric pressure by increasing the oxygen fraction, keeping the alveolar PO2 safe up to approximately 38,000 feet, above which pressure breathing is required.

question_text: The most dangerous symptoms of hypoxia at altitude are
option_a: euphoria and impairment of judgement
option_c: sensation of heat and blurred vision
explanation: The most dangerous aspect of hypoxia is its insidious onset, often accompanied by euphoria (a false sense of well-being) and impaired judgment. This prevents the pilot from recognizing their own deterioration and taking corrective action.

question_text: When consciously breathing fast or hyperventilating due to high arousal or overstress, the carbon dioxide level in the blood is lowered, resulting in:
option_a: less oxygen to be diffused into the cells
option_b: a poor saturation of oxygen in the blood
option_c: a delay in the onset of hypoxia when flying at high altitudes
option_d: the activation of the respiratory centre, which in turn causes hypoxia
explanation: Hyperventilation reduces the carbon dioxide concentration in the blood. This causes blood alkalinity to rise, triggering vasoconstriction of cerebral blood vessels and shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, which reduces oxygen release to the cells.

question_text: With hyperventilation, caused by high levels of arousal or overstress:
option_a: an increased amount of carbon dioxide is exhaled causing muscular spasms and even unconsciousness
option_b: finger nails and lips will turn blue (""cyanosis"")
option_c: more oxygen will reach the brain
option_d: peripherical and scotopic vision will be improved
explanation: The rapid exhalation of carbon dioxide raises blood pH. This results in symptoms such as tingling in the extremities, lightheadedness, muscular spasms, and eventual unconsciousness if breathing is not controlled.

question_text: Breathing 100% oxygen at 38000 ft is equivalent to breathe ambient air at :
explanation: At 38,000 feet, the total barometric pressure is about 200 hPa. Breathing 100% oxygen provides an oxygen partial pressure that matches the partial pressure of oxygen in ambient air at approximately 10,000 feet.

question_text: At what altitude (breathing 100% oxygen without pressure) could symptoms of hypoxia be expected?
option_a: Approximately 38 - 40 000 ft.
explanation: Even when breathing pure oxygen, the total atmospheric pressure above 38,000 to 40,000 feet drops so low that the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli falls below the minimum required to saturate hemoglobin, leading to hypoxia.

question_text: To safely supply the crew with oxygen, at which altitude is it necessary to breathe 100% oxygen plus pressure after a rapid decompression ?
option_a: Approximately 38 000 ft.
explanation: Supplemental oxygen under positive pressure is required above approximately 38,000 feet because the ambient atmospheric pressure is too low to force sufficient oxygen across the alveolar membrane, even when breathing 100% oxygen.

question_text: When the pilot suffers from hypothermia (loss of cabin heating):
option_a: his need for oxygen will be increased as long as he stays conscious
option_b: his oxygen need will not be affected
option_c: his oxygen need will be reduced giving him a better tolerance to hypoxia at higher altitudes
option_d: his oxygen need will be raised and his tolerance to hypoxia will be increased
explanation: Hypothermia causes shivering and increased muscular tension to generate heat, which significantly increases metabolic activity and the body's rate of oxygen consumption, reducing tolerance to hypoxia.

question_text: ""Tunnel vision"" (loss of peripherical vision) can be observed if a pilot is subjected to more than:
explanation: At acceleration levels exceeding +3.5 Gz, blood pools in the lower body, lowering blood pressure at eye level and causing peripheral vision loss (tunnel vision) due to the high sensitivity of the retina to oxygen deprivation.

question_text: ""Grey out"" can be observed if a pilot is subjected to more than:
option_a: + 3 Gz
explanation: Grey out is a temporary visual impairment characterized by a loss of color vision and dimming of the visual field. It occurs when positive vertical acceleration (+Gz) exceeds +3 Gz, reducing blood flow to the eyes before complete blackout.

question_text: The negative (radial) acceleration of an airplane affects the sitting pilot with inertia along :
option_a: the vertical body axis upwards
option_c: the transverse body axis to the right
option_d: the transverse body axis to the left
explanation: Negative radial acceleration (-Gz) acts along the vertical body axis from feet to head. This pushes blood upward into the head and chest, causing a sense of congestion and visual 'red out' due to engorged blood vessels.

question_text: How can a pilot increase his tolerance to +Gz ?
option_a: Tightening of muscles, ducking the head and perform a kind of pressure breathing.
option_d: Relax the muscles, ducking the head and lean upper body forward.
explanation: To increase +Gz tolerance, a pilot can perform the anti-G straining maneuver (AGSM), which involves tensing abdominal and leg muscles to prevent blood pooling, ducking the head, and executing timed, forced exhalations.

question_text: Oxygen in the blood is primarily transported by
option_a: the hemoglobin in the red blood cells
option_c: attaching itself to the hemoglobin in the red blood plasma
option_d: attaching itself to the hemoglobin in the white blood cells
explanation: Oxygen is primarily transported throughout the circulatory system by chemically binding to hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein molecule contained within erythrocytes (red blood cells).

question_text: Large amounts of carbon dioxide are eliminated from the body when hyperventilating. This causes the blood
option_a: to become more alkaline increasing the amount of oxygen to be attached to the hemoglobin at lung area
option_b: to turn more acid thus eliminating more oxygen from the hemoglobin
option_c: to accelerate the oxygen supply to the brain
explanation: Hyperventilation leads to excessive loss of carbon dioxide, making the blood more alkaline. This alkalinity increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (the Bohr effect), preventing oxygen from being easily released to the body's tissues.

question_text: Hypoxia is caused by
option_a: reduced partial oxygen pressure in the lung
option_b: reduced partial pressure of nitrogen in the lung
option_c: an increased number of red blood cells
option_d: a higher affinity of the red blood cells (hemoglobin) to oxygen
explanation: Hypoxic hypoxia is caused by a reduced partial pressure of oxygen in the lungs. This decreases the pressure gradient between the alveoli and pulmonary capillaries, limiting the diffusion of oxygen into the blood.

question_text: Hypoxia can be caused by:1. low partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere when flying at high altitudes without pressurisation and supplemental oxygen2. a decreased saturation of oxygen in the blood due to carbon monoxide attached to the hemoglobin3. blood pooling in the lower extremities due to inertia (+ Gz)4. malfunction of the body cells to metabolize oxygen (i.e. after a hangover)
option_a: 1, 2, 3 and 4 are correct
option_b: 1 and 2 are correct, 3 and 4 are false
explanation: Hypoxia can occur through oxygen deficiency in the air (hypoxic), carbon monoxide blocking hemoglobin (hypemic), pooling of blood during high-G maneuvers (stagnant), or alcohol interfering with cellular metabolism (histotoxic).

question_text: A pilot will get hypoxia
option_a: after decompression at high altitude and not taking additional oxygen in time
option_b: after decompression to 30 000 feet and taking 100 % oxygen via an oxygen mask
option_c: if his rate of climb exceeds 5 000 ft/min
option_d: if he is flying an unpressurized airplane at an altitude of 15 000 feet and breathing 100 % oxygen
explanation: A rapid decompression at high altitudes causes an immediate drop in cabin pressure and partial pressure of oxygen. Without rapid access to emergency oxygen, a pilot will quickly develop acute hypoxia.

question_text: Why is hypoxia especially dangerous for pilots flying solo?
option_a: Since the first signs of hypoxia are generally hard to detect (hypoxia of the brain), the solo pilot may not be able to react in time (i.e. activate his emergency oxygen system)
option_b: Hypoxia does not cause a loss of control in steering the plane.
option_c: Hypoxia improves vision at night, so the pilot will have no indication of danger.
option_d: The pilot may loose control when he is using the oxygen mask.
explanation: Hypoxia impairs cognitive function, self-monitoring, and judgment early on, often accompanied by a false sense of well-being (euphoria), which makes it highly dangerous for a solo pilot who may not realize the need to take action.

question_text: In the following list you find some symptoms for hypoxia and carbon monoxide poisoning. Please mark those indicating hypoxia:
option_a: Visual disturbances, lack of concentration, euphoria.
explanation: The initial symptoms of hypoxia include visual disturbances (such as tunnel vision or loss of night vision), lack of concentration, and euphoria, all of which compromise flight safety.

question_text: Which of the following is a/are symptom(s) of hypoxia ?
option_a: Lack of concentration, fatigue, euphoria
option_d: Excessive rate and depth of breathing combined with pains in the chest area
explanation: Common symptoms of hypoxic hypoxia include decreased cognitive concentration, physical fatigue, and euphoria, which are particularly insidious as they prevent the pilot from recognizing their own physiological decline.

question_text: A symptom comparison for hypoxia and hyperventilation is:
option_a: cyanosis (blue color of finger-nail and lips) exists only in hypoxia
option_b: there are great differences between the two
option_c: altitude hypoxia is very unlikely at cabin pressure altitudes above 10 000 ft
option_d: symptoms caused by hyperventilation will immediately vanish when 100% oxygen is given
explanation: Cyanosis, the bluish discoloration of the skin, lips, and fingernail beds, is caused by a high concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the blood, which is a symptom unique to hypoxia and does not occur in hyperventilation.

question_text: Which statement applies to hypoxia?
option_a: sensitivity and reaction to hypoxia varies from person to person
option_b: carbon monoxide increases the tolerance of the brain to oxygen deficiency
option_c: you may become immune to hypoxia when exposed repeatedly to hypoxia
option_d: it is possible to prognose when, how and where hypoxia reaction starts to set in
explanation: Susceptibility to hypoxia is highly individual and varies daily based on factors such as physical fitness, fatigue, tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and altitude acclimatization.

question_text: Hypoxia can also be caused by
option_a: a lack of red blood cells in the blood or decreased ability of the hemoglobin to transport oxygen
option_b: a lack of nitrogen in ambient air
option_c: too much carbon dioxide in the blood
option_d: increasing oxygen partial pressure used for the exchange of gases
explanation: Hypemic hypoxia occurs when the blood's capacity to transport oxygen is reduced. This can be caused by anemia, blood loss, or carbon monoxide poisoning which reduces the amount of functional hemoglobin available.

question_text: Which symptom of hypoxia is the most dangerous for conducting safe flight ?
option_a: The interference of reasoning and perceptive functions.
explanation: Impairment of cognitive reasoning, judgment, and perceptive functions are the most dangerous symptoms of hypoxia. They prevent the pilot from recognizing their errors or executing corrective procedures.

question_text: Which of the following applies to carbon monoxide poisoning?
option_a: Several days are needed to recuperate from a carbon monoxide poisoning.
option_b: A very early symptom for realising carbon monoxide poisoning is euphoria.
option_c: The human body shows no sign of carbon monoxide poisoning.
option_d: Inhaling carbon monoxide leads to hyperventilation.
explanation: Carbon monoxide binds with hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin, which is highly stable and has a long half-life. It takes several days of breathing fresh air or oxygen to fully eliminate carbon monoxide from the body.

question_text: The momentum of gas exchange in respiration is
option_a: dependent on the pressure gradient between the participating gases during respiration
option_b: the excess pressure caused by inhaling
option_c: independent from the partial pressures of the participating gases
option_d: depending on the active transportation of nitrogen into the alveoli
explanation: The passive diffusion of gases across the alveolar-capillary membrane is driven by the partial pressure gradient of each gas, moving from an area of higher partial pressure to one of lower partial pressure.

question_text: Which component(s) is/are transporting the oxygen in the blood?
option_a: Hemoglobin in the red blood cells.
explanation: Oxygen is transported from the lungs to the body tissues by binding to hemoglobin molecules inside red blood cells, with only a very small fraction dissolved in the blood plasma.

question_text: Affinity to hemoglobin is best with:
option_a: carbon monoxide
explanation: Hemoglobin has an affinity for carbon monoxide that is over 200 times stronger than its affinity for oxygen. Even trace amounts of CO will displace oxygen and drastically reduce the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

question_text: Which of the following is true concerning carbon monoxide?
option_a: It is to be found in the smoke of cigarettes lifting up a smoker's ""physiological altitude"".

explanation: Aerotitis (middle ear barotrauma) is characterized by a sensation of fullness, pain, and temporary hearing difficulties, whereas aerosinusitis (sinus barotrauma) causes localized facial pain without hearing impairment.

question_text: How can you determine if a person is suffering from a barotrauma of the sinuses of the nose (aerosinusitis) or the middle ear (aerotitis) ?
option_a: Hearing difficulties will normally accompany aerotitis

explanation: If a pilot experiences severe middle ear barotrauma during descent, they should stop descending, climb to a higher altitude to equalize pressure, and then descend at a much slower rate.

question_text: Please mark the counter-measure a pilot can use against a barotrauma of the middle ear (aerotitis).
option_a: Stop descending, climb again and then descend with reduced sink rate
explanation: Middle ear barotrauma (aerotitis) is most likely to occur during rapid descents. This is because the increasing ambient pressure forces the tympanic membrane inward if the Eustachian tube fails to open and equalize pressure.

question_text: Barotrauma of the middle ear most likely will occur

explanation: A barotrauma of the middle ear occurs when pressure cannot equalize during descent, resulting in the tympanic membrane being stretched inward, causing pain and a noticeable reduction in hearing ability.

explanation: Early signs of hyperventilation include dizziness, lightheadedness, tingling in the extremities (paresthesia), and muscle twitching, which result from decreased carbon dioxide levels in the blood.

question_text: Which of the following symptoms can mark a beginning hyperventilation?
option_a: Dizzy feeling
option_d: Cyanosis (blueing of lips and finger nails)
explanation: A beginning stage of hyperventilation is marked by symptoms such as dizziness and tingling in the fingers and lips. These symptoms are caused by the respiratory alkalosis that accompanies rapid breathing.

question_text: Out of the list of possible measures to counteract hyperventilation, the most effective measure against hyperventilation tetany is:
option_a: breathe into a plastic or paper bag
option_d: speak soothingly and get the person to breathe slowly
explanation: Breathing into a paper or plastic bag forces the patient to re-breathe their exhaled carbon dioxide. This increases the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the blood, reversing the alkalosis and stopping muscular spasms (tetany).

question_text: What event can cause a hyperventilation (not required by physical need)?1. Pressure breathing.2. Anxiety or fear.3. Overstress.4. Strong pain.5. Jogging.
option_a: 1,2,3 and 4 are correct, 5 is false
explanation: Hyperventilation can be triggered by pressure breathing, anxiety, fear, overstress, or severe pain, which cause a psychological or mechanical disruption of normal breathing. Physical exercise like jogging causes hyperpnea, which is a normal metabolic need.

question_text: Which of the following could a pilot experience when he is hyperventilating?1. Dizziness2. Muscular spasms3. Visual disturbances4. Cyanosis
option_a: 1,2 and 3 are correct, 4 is false
option_c: 1 is false, all others are correct
explanation: Dizziness, muscular spasms, and visual disturbances are classic symptoms of hyperventilation due to hypocapnia-induced cerebral vasoconstriction. Cyanosis is a symptom of oxygen deficiency and occurs in hypoxia, not hyperventilation.

question_text: TUC (Time of Useful Consciousness) is:
option_a: the length of time during which an individual can act with both mental and physical efficiency and alertness, measured from the moment at which he is exposed to hypoxia
option_b: the time before becoming unconscious at a sudden pressure loss
option_c: the time after pressure loss until decompression sickness sets in
option_d: the time between the start of hypoxia and death
explanation: Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) is the length of time a pilot can perform their duties with mental and physical efficiency after being deprived of adequate oxygen, before cognitive incapacitation occurs.

question_text: The ""Effective Performance Time"" or ""Time of Useful Consciousness"" after a decompression at 35 000 ft is:
option_a: between 30 and 60 seconds
explanation: At 35,000 feet, the Time of Useful Consciousness is between 30 and 60 seconds. Following a rapid decompression, this time can be cut in half due to the rapid expansion and exit of air from the lungs.

question_text: The time between inadequate oxygen supply and incapacitation is called TUC (Time of Useful Consciousness). It
option_a: varies individually and depends on cabin pressure altitude
option_b: is the same amount of time for every person
option_c: is not dependent on physical or psychological pressure
option_d: varies individually and does not depend on altitude
explanation: The Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) varies between individuals based on physical fitness, fatigue, and smoking habits, and is highly dependent on the cabin pressure altitude reached.

question_text: After a decompression to 43 000 FT the TUC (Time of Useful Consciousness) will be approximately:
option_a: 5-15 seconds
explanation: At 43,000 feet, the ambient pressure is extremely low, and the blood-gas pressure gradient in the lungs is reversed. This leads to a very short Time of Useful Consciousness of approximately 5 to 15 seconds.

question_text: Flights immediately after SCUBA-diving (compressed gas mixtures, bottles) (>10 m depth)
option_a: are forbidden
option_b: can be performed without any danger
option_c: are allowed, if 38000 FT are not exceeded
option_d: should be avoided because hypoxia may develop
explanation: Flying immediately after SCUBA diving is forbidden because the high pressure of underwater diving saturates body tissues with nitrogen. When climbing to altitude, the drop in pressure causes this nitrogen to form bubbles, leading to decompression sickness.

question_text: Pain in the Joints (""bends""), which suddenly appear during a flight , are symptoms of
option_a: decompression sickness
explanation: Joint pain, known as 'the bends,' is a classic symptom of decompression sickness. It is caused by nitrogen bubbles coming out of solution and accumulating in the joint capsules, tendons, and surrounding tissues.

question_text: After a cabin pressure loss in approximately 35 000 FT the TUC (Time of Useful Consciousness) will be approximately:
option_a: 30 -90 seconds
explanation: At a cabin altitude of 35,000 feet, the typical Time of Useful Consciousness ranges from 30 to 90 seconds. This time can be significantly shorter depending on individual health factors and the speed of decompression.

question_text: You suffered a rapid decompression without the appearance of any decompression sickness symptoms.How long should you wait until your next flight?
option_a: 12 hours
explanation: Even if a pilot is asymptomatic after a rapid decompression, they must wait at least 12 hours before their next flight. This allows any micro-bubbles of nitrogen that formed in the blood or tissues to safely dissolve and clear.

question_text: Flying immediately following a dive with SCUBA diving equipment (> 10 m depth)
option_a: can cause decompression sicknesss even when flying at pressure altitudes below 18 000 FT
option_b: prevents any dangers caused by aeroembolism (decompression sickness) when climbing to altitudes not exceeding 30 000 FT
option_c: has no influence on altitude flights
option_d: is forbidden for the flight crew, because it leads to hypoxia
explanation: SCUBA diving saturates body tissues with excess nitrogen. Subsequent flights within 24 hours can trigger decompression sickness (aeroembolism) even at low cabin pressure altitudes below 18,000 feet.

question_text: Barotrauma of the sinuses of the nose (aerosinusitis)
option_a: is caused by a difference in pressure existing between the sinus cavity and the ambient air
option_b: is only caused by the flying sport, not by the diving sport
option_c: is an irritation of sinuses by abuse of nose sprays
option_d: is only caused by colds and their effects
explanation: Aerosinusitis (sinus barotrauma) is caused by a difference in air pressure between the sinus cavities and the ambient atmosphere. If a sinus duct is blocked, pressure cannot equalize, leading to severe pain and tissue irritation.

question_text: Barodontalgia
option_a: arises especially with irritations of the sensitive tissues close to the root of a tooth
option_b: arises only at higher altitudes and after decompression
option_d: arises in combination with a cold and very high rates of descent
explanation: Barodontalgia (tooth squeeze) is caused by trapped air pockets in dental restorations or root infections. As ambient pressure decreases during climb, the trapped gas expands, pressing on sensitive tooth nerves and causing sharp pain.

question_text: At a high altitude flight (no cabin pressure system available), a pilot gets severe flatulence due to trapped gases. The correct counter-measure is:
option_a: descend to lower altitude
explanation: If a pilot experiences severe flatulence or abdominal pain from expanding gases at high altitude, the correct corrective action is to descend to a lower altitude, increasing ambient pressure and compressing the trapped gas.

question_text: A barotrauma of the middle ear (aerotitis)
option_a: is more likely, when the pilot is flying with a respiratory infection and during descent
option_b: is only caused by large pressure changes during climb
option_c: causes severe pain in the sinuses
option_d: is to be expected during rapid decompressions, but an emergency descent immediately following the decompression will eliminate the problem
explanation: Aerotitis (middle ear barotrauma) is highly likely to occur during descent if the pilot has a cold. Swollen tissues block the Eustachian tube, preventing ambient air from entering the middle ear to equalize pressure.

question_text: Trapped intestinal gases can cause severe pain. When is this the case?
option_a: More frequent when flying above 18 000 FT in a non-pressurized aircraft.
option_c: Only in pressurized aircraft when flying at higher flight levels.
option_d: During descent as well as during climb, when the cabin pressure altitude is exceeding 2 000 FT
explanation: Expanded intestinal gases follow Boyle's Law. Above 18,000 feet, ambient pressure is halved, causing trapped gas to double in volume, which can cause severe pain and incapacitation in a non-pressurized aircraft.

question_text: The risk of a barotrauma of the middle ear is more likely to occur
option_a: with colds and rapid descents
explanation: The risk of middle ear barotrauma (aerotitis) increases significantly during a rapid descent when the pilot has a cold, because inflamed nasal tissues prevent the Eustachian tube from opening to equalize pressure.

question_text: Equalization of pressure is limited between the middle ear and the ambient, when:
option_a: the eustachian tube is blocked
explanation: Pressure equalization between the middle ear cavity and the ambient atmosphere becomes restricted or impossible when the Eustachian tube is blocked by mucus or inflammation.

question_text: A barotrauma of the middle ear is
option_a: an acute or chronic trauma of the middle ear caused by a difference of pressure on either side of the eardrum
option_b: a bacterial infection of the middle ear
option_c: a dilatation of the eustachian tube
option_d: an infection of the middle ear caused by rapid decompression
explanation: Barotrauma of the middle ear (aerotitis media) is an acute or chronic injury caused by a pressure differential across the eardrum, stretching it and causing pain or potential rupture.

question_text: The eustachian tube is the passage way between the
option_a: nasopharynx and the middle ear
option_c: nose, pharynx and the external auditory canal
explanation: The Eustachian tube is a small physiological channel that connects the nasopharynx (upper throat) to the middle ear cavity, serving to equalize pressure across the tympanic membrane.

question_text: Which part of the ear could be affected due to air pressure changes during climb and/or descent?
option_a: The eustachian tube and the tympanic membrane (ear drum)
explanation: Pressure changes during climb and descent primarily affect the Eustachian tube and the tympanic membrane (eardrum) as the ear attempts to equalize pressure between the middle ear cavity and the outside air.

question_text: Hypoxia effects visual performance.A pilot may:
option_a: get blurred and/or tunnel vision
option_b: have a reduction of 25% in visual acuity at 8000 FT AGL
option_c: be unable to maintain piercing vision below 5000 FT AGL
option_d: get colour blindness accompanied by severe headache
explanation: Hypoxia impairs night vision, peripheral vision (tunnel vision), and visual acuity by depriving the highly oxygen-demanding retina and visual cortex of necessary oxygen.

question_text: Which of the following symptoms could a pilot get, when he is subjected to hypoxia?1. Fatigue.2. Euphoria.3. Lack of concentration.4. Pain in the joints.5. Sensation of suffocation.
option_a: 1, 2 and 3 are correct
explanation: Common symptoms of hypoxic hypoxia include physical fatigue, a false sense of well-being (euphoria), and a loss of cognitive concentration, all of which compromise flight safety.

question_text: In relation to hypoxia, which of the following paraphrase(s) is (are) correct?
option_a: This is a physical condition caused by a lack of oxygen to meet the needs of the body tissues, leading to mental and muscular disturbances, causing impaired thinking, poor judgement and slow reactions
option_b: This is a condition of lacking oxygen in the brain causing the circulatory system to compensate by decreasing the heart rate.
option_c: Hypoxia is often produced during steep turns when pilots turn their heads in a direction opposite to the direction in which the aircraft is turning
option_d: This is a physical condition caused by a lack of oxygen saturation in the blood while hyperventilating.
explanation: Hypoxia is a physiological condition caused by a lack of oxygen in the body tissues. It leads to mental and muscular impairment, causing poor judgment, slowed reaction times, and eventual unconsciousness.

question_text: Hyperventilation is due to an excessive rate of breathing and can produce the following symptoms:
option_a: dizziness, tingling sensation in the fingers and toes, nausea and blurred vision
option_b: reduced heart rate and increase in visual acuity
option_c: a state of overconfidence and reduced heart rate
explanation: Hyperventilation reduces carbon dioxide in the blood, causing alkalosis. This results in symptoms like dizziness, tingling in the fingers and toes (paresthesia), mild nausea, and blurred vision.

question_text: In order to get rid of excess nitrogen following scuba diving, subsequent flights should be delayed
option_a: 24 hours
option_d: 48 hours after a continuous ascent in the water has been made
explanation: To ensure that excess nitrogen absorbed during SCUBA diving is safely eliminated from the body, pilots should delay subsequent flights by at least 24 hours.

question_text: The cabin pressure in airline operation is
option_a: normally not exceeding 6 000 to 8 000 feet
explanation: Commercial aircraft cabin pressure systems are designed to maintain a comfortable pressure altitude, which is normally regulated to not exceed a cabin altitude of 6,000 to 8,000 feet.

question_text: The type of hypoxia, which occurs at altitude is a explained by:
option_a: Dalton´s law
explanation: Hypoxic hypoxia at altitude is explained by Dalton's law of partial pressures. As total atmospheric pressure decreases, the partial pressure of oxygen decreases proportionally, reducing oxygen uptake in the lungs.

question_text: Gaseous exchange in the human body depends on:1. diffusion gradients between the participating gases2. permeable membranes3. partial pressure of oxygen in the alveolus air4. acid-base balance in the blood
option_a: 1, 2, 3 and 4 are correct
explanation: Gaseous exchange in the lungs is governed by gas diffusion gradients, membrane permeability, the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli, and the acid-base balance of the blood.

question_text: Hyperventilation causes
option_a: a lack of carbon dioxide in the blood
option_b: an excess of carbon dioxide in the blood
explanation: Hyperventilation is defined as breathing in excess of metabolic needs. This causes the rapid elimination of carbon dioxide from the blood, resulting in hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis.

question_text: Anxiety and fear can cause
option_a: hyperventilation
explanation: Psychological factors like sudden anxiety, panic, or fear trigger the sympathetic nervous system to increase breathing rate and depth, which can lead to hyperventilation.

question_text: Symptoms of decompression sickness
option_a: sometimes can appear with a delay after the airplane is on the ground
option_b: always begin immediately after the decompression during the flight
option_c: normally take 2 or 3 days to appear after exposure to a hypobaric atmosphere
option_d: disappear on landing and never appear again
explanation: Decompression sickness symptoms can sometimes manifest with a delay after the aircraft has landed on the ground, as nitrogen bubbles may continue to form and grow in the body tissues over time.

question_text: The first effect to be noticed on gradual exposure to high positive radial accelerations is
option_a: grey-out
explanation: During gradual exposure to positive vertical acceleration (+Gz), the first visual symptom to be noticed is grey-out, which is a loss of color vision and dimming of the visual field before blackout occurs.

question_text: Decompression sickness occurs in association with exposure to reduced atmospheric pressure.The evolution of bubbles of nitrogen coming out of solution in body tissues can be derived from:
option_a: Henry´s law
explanation: Decompression sickness and the formation of nitrogen bubbles in body tissues due to a drop in ambient pressure is governed by Henry's law, which relates gas solubility to partial pressure.

question_text: The normal rate of breathing is
option_a: 20 to 30 cycles a minute
explanation: The normal respiratory rate for a healthy adult at rest is approximately 12 to 16 cycles (breaths) per minute, adjusting automatically to maintain blood carbon dioxide balance.

question_text: The main function of the red blood cells is
option_a: to transport oxygen
option_b: to participate in the process of coagulation of the blood
option_c: the cellular defense of the organism
option_d: to contribute to the immune response of the organism
explanation: The primary function of erythrocytes (red blood cells) is to transport oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues, using the iron-bearing protein hemoglobin.

question_text: Altitude-hypoxia, when breathing ambient air, should not occur (indifferent phase)
option_a: below 3 000 m
explanation: At altitudes below 3,000 meters (approximately 10,000 feet), the human body can easily compensate for the slight decrease in oxygen partial pressure, so altitude-hypoxia does not normally occur.

question_text: ""The Bends"" as a symptom of decompression sickness consists of:
option_a: pain in the joints
option_b: pain in the thorax and a backing cough
explanation: The 'bends' is a localized form of decompression sickness where nitrogen bubbles form in the joint cavities and surrounding tendons, causing severe, aching pain.

question_text: One of the most frequent symptom(s) of decompression sickness emerging after a decompression in airline operation
option_a: are the bends
option_d: are neurological damages to the CNS
explanation: In aviation operations, the most common clinical symptom of altitude decompression sickness is 'the bends,' which presents as musculoskeletal and joint pain.

question_text: Which phenomenon is common to hypoxia and hyperventilation?
option_a: Tingling sensations in arms or legs.
explanation: A common symptom shared by both hypoxia and hyperventilation is a tingling sensation in the arms, legs, and extremities, resulting from altered peripheral nerve excitability.

question_text: 1. Euphoria can be a symptom of hypoxia. 2. Someone in an euphoric condition is more prone to error.
option_a: 1 and 2 are both correct
explanation: Euphoria is a dangerous symptom of hypoxia because it causes a false sense of well-being and security, making the pilot highly prone to critical errors in judgment.

question_text: Incapacitation caused by barotrauma from gaseous expansion after decompression at high altitude may be associated with the following part(s) of the body:1 the digestive tract2 the ears3 the eyes4 the sinuses
explanation: Barotrauma from gaseous expansion after decompression causes immediate distension and severe pain in the digestive tract, which can lead to physical incapacitation.

question_text: Of the following alternatives, which objective effects are due to positive acceleration (+ Gz)?- 1: Decrease in heart rate- 2: Pooling of blood into lower parts of the body- 3: Drop in blood pressure above heart-level- 4: Downward displacement or deformation of soft or mobile organs
explanation: Positive vertical acceleration (+Gz) pools blood in the lower body, drops blood pressure above heart level, and causes downward displacement of internal organs. This triggers a compensatory increase in heart rate.

question_text: What is hypoxia ?
option_a: Any condition where the oxygen concentration of the body is below normal limits or where the oxygen available to the body cannot be used due to some pathological condition
option_b: The total absence of oxygen in the air
option_c: The respiratory symptom associated with altitude decompression sickness
option_d: A state charcterised by an excessive supply of oxygen which may be due to maladjustment of the mask
explanation: Hypoxia is defined as any condition where the oxygen concentration in the body tissues is below normal, or where the available oxygen cannot be utilized by the cells due to pathological factors.

question_text: What could be symptoms of hypoxia (when flying without oxygen) above 12,000 ft?
option_a: Headache, fatigue, dizziness, lack of coordination
option_c: Euphoria, headache, improvement in judgement, loss of consciousness
option_d: Trembling, increase in body temperature, convulsions,slowing of the rate of breathing
explanation: Above 12,000 feet, exposure to hypoxia impairs cerebral function, leading to symptoms such as headache, physical fatigue, dizziness, and a lack of motor coordination.

explanation: This question appears to be incomplete in the original syllabus. In physiological terms, climbing from sea level to higher altitudes causes a decrease in ambient atmospheric pressure and partial pressure of oxygen.

question_text: Physiological problems due to increasing altitude are caused by :
option_a: decreased atmospherical pressure
explanation: Physiological problems like hypoxia and barotrauma associated with increasing flight altitudes are directly caused by the decrease in ambient atmospheric pressure.

question_text: Air at an altitude of 18.000 feet contains, approximately :
option_a: 21% oxygen
explanation: At an altitude of 18,000 feet, the ambient air contains approximately 21% oxygen by volume, which is the same proportion as at sea level, although the density and pressure are halved.

question_text: Dry air is a mixture of gases. Their volume percentage is about:
option_a: 21% oxygen,78% nitrogen, 1% other gases
explanation: Dry air in the Earth's lower atmosphere is a mixture composed of approximately 21% oxygen, 78% nitrogen, and 1% of trace gases (primarily argon and carbon dioxide).

question_text: The occurrence of pain in the joints (bends) during decompression can be explained by the principle that:
option_a: the quantity of a gas dissolved in a fluid is proportional to the pressure of that gas above the fluid (Henry's Law)
option_b: a volume of gas is inversely proportional to the pressure of this gas at constant temperature (Boyle's law)
option_c: the total pressure of a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the separate gases (Dalton's Law)
option_d: the molecules of a gas will move from an area of higher concentration or partial pressure to an area of lower concentration or partial pressure (law of diffusion)
explanation: Henry's law states that the mass of a gas dissolved in a given volume of liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas. Upon decompression, ambient pressure drops and dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution, causing joint pain (the bends).

question_text: Pain in the joints caused by gas bubbles following a decompression is called:
option_a: bends
explanation: Decompression sickness (DCS) occurs when nitrogen bubbles form in body fluids and tissues due to a rapid pressure drop, with joint pain specifically referred to as 'the bends.'

question_text: What are the main clinical signs of hypoxia during explosive decompression ?
option_a: Increase in heart and respiratory rates, euphoria, impairment of judgement, memory disorders
option_c: Increase in heart rate, decrease in body temperature impairment of judgement
option_d: Headaches, articular pain, speeding-up of the respiratory rate, memory disorders
explanation: Explosive decompression triggers acute hypoxic hypoxia, characterized by a rapid increase in heart and respiration rates as the body attempts to compensate, alongside mental confusion, euphoria, and memory loss.

question_text: Which is the procedure to be followed when symptoms of decompression sickness occur?
option_a: Descend to the lowest possible level and land as soon as possible
option_b: Descend to the lowest possible level and wait for the symptoms to disappear before climbing again
option_c: Only medical treatment is of use
option_d: Only the prompt supply of oxygen is necessary
explanation: If a pilot or passenger displays symptoms of decompression sickness, the pilot must immediately descend to the lowest safe altitude and land as soon as possible to seek medical evaluation and hyperbaric treatment.

question_text: What is decompression sickness ?
option_a: An sickness resulting from the formation of nitrogen bubbles in bodily tissues and fluids after a cabin pressure loss at high altitude
option_b: A frequent disorder in commercial aviation due to the pressurisation curve of modern aircraft
option_c: A disorder which is solely encountered below 18,000 ft
option_d: The formation of air bubbles in bodily tissues, with no consequences for people's capabilities
explanation: Decompression sickness is a systemic condition resulting from the formation of nitrogen bubbles in body tissues and blood when cabin pressure is lost at high altitudes (typically above 18,000 feet).

question_text: Which of the following statements are correct:-1: Scuba diving may be practiced without restriction-2: Many medicines have effects which are incompatible with flight safety-3: An adequate amount of fluid should be drunk when flying-4: Diet has no repercussion on health
option_a: 2 and 3 are correct
explanation: Aviation medicine warns that many common over-the-counter and prescription medications have side effects incompatible with flight safety, and adequate hydration is critical when flying to prevent dehydration.

question_text: A pressurized cabin helps to prevent:1. decompression sickness2 .the problem of expansion of gases in the intestines3. hypoxia4. coronary desease
option_a: 1, 2 and 3 are correct.
explanation: A pressurized cabin maintains an artificial environment that prevents hypoxic hypoxia, decompression sickness, and the painful expansion of trapped gastrointestinal gases by keeping the cabin altitude low.

question_text: Healthy people are usually capable to compensate for a lack of oxygen up to
explanation: A healthy, unacclimatized individual can typically compensate for the reduced partial pressure of oxygen up to altitudes of approximately 10,000 to 12,000 feet through minor increases in cardiac output and respiration.

question_text: When flying above 10.000 feet hypoxia arises because:
option_a: the partial oxygen pressure is lower than at sea level.
option_b: the composition of the blood changes
option_c: the composition of the air is different from sea level
option_d: the percentage of oxygen is lower than at sea level
explanation: Hypoxia occurs at altitudes above 10,000 feet because the ambient atmospheric pressure decreases, reducing the partial pressure of oxygen in the inspired air and lungs, even though the oxygen percentage remains constant at 21%.

question_text: Saturation of oxygen in the blood at sea level is 98%. This saturation decreases with:1. decreasing air pressure2. carbon monoxide poisoning3. increasing altitude4. increasing air pressure
option_a: 1, 2 and 3 are correct, 4 is false
explanation: The oxygen saturation of arterial blood, normally around 98% at sea level, decreases with a drop in ambient air pressure, carbon monoxide poisoning (which blocks hemoglobin), and climbing to higher altitudes.

question_text: Hypoxia is a situation in which the cells
option_a: have a shortage of oxygen
option_d: have a shortage of carbon dioxide
explanation: Hypoxia is a physiological condition defined by an insufficient concentration of oxygen in the body's cells and tissues to support normal metabolic function.

question_text: The severity of hypoxia depends on the:1. rate of decompression2. physical fitness3. flight level4. individual tolerance
option_a: 1,2,3 and 4 are correct
option_d: 1 and 3 are correct, 2 and 4 are false
explanation: The severity and onset of hypoxia depend on multiple factors, including the rate of decompression, the altitude (flight level), individual physiological tolerance, and physical fitness.

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning hypoxia is correct?
option_a: It is a potential threat to safety.
option_b: It is never a problem at altitudes below 25.000 ft.
option_c: It activates the senses and makes them function better.
option_d: It has little effect on the body, because the body can always compensate for it.
explanation: Hypoxia represents a significant and potential threat to flight safety because it impairs cognitive performance, judgment, and situational awareness without the pilot's conscious realization.

question_text: Early symptoms of hypoxia could be: 1. euphoria 2. decreased rate and depth of breathing 3. lack of concentration 4. visual disturbances
option_a: 1,3 and 4 are correct
explanation: Early symptoms of hypoxia are insidious and include a false sense of security (euphoria), cognitive decline (lack of concentration), and visual disturbances like tunnel vision or loss of night vision.

question_text: One of the most dangerous symptoms of hypoxia concerning flight safety is:
option_a: impaired judgement, disabling the pilot to recognize the symptoms
option_b: reduced coordination of limb movements, causing the pilot to spin
option_c: cyanosis, reducing then pilots ability to hear
explanation: The most hazardous aspect of hypoxia is the impairment of cognitive judgment and reasoning, which prevents a pilot from recognizing their own symptoms or taking timely corrective actions.

question_text: Which of the following symptoms can indicate the beginning of hypoxia?1. Blue lips and finger nails.2. Euphoria.3. Flatulence.4 .Unconsciousness..
option_a: 1, 2 and 4 are correct.
explanation: Early warning signs of hypoxic hypoxia include cyanosis (blue discoloration of the lips and fingernails due to deoxygenated hemoglobin), euphoria, and eventual loss of consciousness.

question_text: Among the functions below, which is the most sensitive to hypoxia?
option_a: Night vision.
explanation: Night vision is the sensory function most sensitive to oxygen deprivation, with noticeable degradation in visual acuity and contrast sensitivity occurring at altitudes as low as 5,000 feet.

question_text: You are crossing the Alps in a non-pressurised aircraft at an altitude of 15.000 feet. You do not use the oxygen mask because you feel fine. This is unsafe, because:
option_a: your judgement could be impaired
option_b: the blood-pressure can get too high
option_c: the blood-pressure can get too low
explanation: Flying at 15,000 feet in an unpressurized aircraft without supplemental oxygen is extremely dangerous because hypoxic hypoxia will impair judgment, rendering the pilot unable to assess their own deteriorating state.

question_text: During a night flight at 10,000 feet you notice that your acuity of vision has decreased. In this case you can increase your acuity by:
option_a: breathing extra oxygen through the oxygen mask.
option_c: scanning sectors of the field of vision
explanation: Because night vision is highly sensitive to hypoxia, breathing supplemental oxygen at altitudes as low as 10,000 feet is an effective way to restore visual acuity and contrast sensitivity during night operations.

question_text: During flight all crewmembers have one or more of the following symptoms: 1. blue lips 2. mental disturbances 3. tingling sensations in arms and/or legs 4. reduction of peripheral visionWhich is the possible cause?
option_a: Hypoxia.
explanation: The combination of blue lips (cyanosis), cognitive impairment, tingling sensations (paresthesia), and loss of peripheral vision in flight crew is a clear indication of hypoxic hypoxia.

question_text: Which measure(s) will help to compensate hypoxia?1. Descend below 10 000 FT.2. Breathe 100 % oxygen.3. Climb to or above 10 000 FT.4. Reduce physical activities.
option_a: 1, 2 and 4 are correct
option_d: 1 and 2 are correct, 3 and 4 are false
explanation: To resolve hypoxia in flight, a pilot must immediately descend below 10,000 feet, breathe 100% supplemental oxygen, and minimize physical exertion to reduce the body's oxygen demand.

question_text: Hypoxia can be prevented when the pilot
option_a: is using additional oxygen when flying above 10.000 feet
option_b: is relying on the body's built in warning system recognizing any stage of hypoxia
option_c: is swallowing, yawing and applying the Valsalva method
option_d: will not exceed 20 000 FT cabin pressure altitude
explanation: Hypoxia can be reliably prevented by using supplemental oxygen or ensuring the cabin pressurization system maintains a cabin altitude below 10,000 feet.

question_text: Hypoxia can occur because:
option_a: you are hyperventilating
option_b: you are getting toomuch solar radiation
option_d: the percentage of oxygen is lower at altitude
explanation: Although the volume percentage of oxygen remains 21% at altitude, the total atmospheric pressure is lower, reducing the oxygen partial pressure. Hyperventilation can also lead to cerebral hypoxia due to hypocapnia-induced vasoconstriction.

question_text: You should not despense blood without prior information from your flight surgeon. The most important reason for this advise is:
option_a: you are more susceptible to hypoxia after a blood-donation.
option_b: the chance you get the bends is higher after blood-donation
option_c: your blood-pressure is too low after blood-donation
option_d: your heart frequency is too low after blood-donation
explanation: Aviation regulations require pilots to wait after donating blood because the temporary loss of red blood cells reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, making them highly susceptible to hypoxia at altitude.

question_text: Hyperventilation is:
option_a: an increased lung ventilation
option_b: a too high percentage of nitrogen in the blood
option_d: a too high percentage of oxygen in the blood.
explanation: Hyperventilation is defined as an increase in alveolar ventilation that exceeds the body's metabolic demand, leading to the excessive elimination of carbon dioxide from the blood.

question_text: Hyperventilation is:
option_a: a normal compensatory physiological reaction to a drop in partial oxygen pressure (i.e. when climbing a high mountain)
option_b: an accellerated heart frequency caused by an increasing blood pressure
option_c: an accellerated heart frequency caused by a decreasing blood-pressure
option_d: a reduction of partial oxygen pressure in the brain
explanation: Hyperventilation is an involuntary physiological reaction where the respiratory rate and depth increase. While it occurs pathologically due to anxiety, it is also a normal compensatory response to the drop in oxygen partial pressure at altitude.

question_text: What is the procedure above 10.000 ft altitude when faced with explosive decompression?
option_a: Don an oxygen mask and descend to below 10,000 ft
option_c: Descend to below 10,000 ft and signal an emergency
option_d: Check the cabin altitude, don an oxygen mask and maintain level flight
explanation: Following an explosive decompression at altitudes above 10,000 feet, the immediate action is to don an oxygen mask to prevent rapid incapacitation, followed by an emergency descent to a safe altitude below 10,000 feet.

question_text: What is the average Time of Useful Consciousness after a rapid decompression at 40,000 ft ?
option_a: About 12 seconds
explanation: At 40,000 feet, the Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) following a rapid decompression is extremely short, typically lasting only about 12 seconds due to the rapid loss of alveolar oxygen tension.

question_text: What is the Time of Useful Consciouness ?
option_a: The length of time during which an individualcan act with both mental and physical efficiency and alertness, measured from the moment at which he loses his available oxygen supply
option_b: The time taken to become aware of hypoxia due to gradual decompression
option_c: The pilot's reaction time when faced with hypoxia
option_d: The period of time between the start of hypoxia and the moment that the pilot becomes aware of it
explanation: Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) is the duration from the loss of oxygen supply during which an individual can still perform flight tasks with cognitive alertness and motor coordination.

question_text: Which of the folllowing statements concerning barotrauma are correct? They are:
option_a: due to pressure differentials between gases in hollow cavities of the body and the ambient pressure
option_b: caused by an increase in the partial pressure of oxygen associated with a decrease in altitude
option_c: more likely to occur during ascent then during a rapid descent
option_d: mainly associated with a sink rate which exceeds the ability of the body to balance its internal pressures
explanation: Barotraumas are physical injuries caused by pressure differentials that develop between air trapped in body cavities (such as the middle ear, sinuses, and digestive tract) and the external environment.

question_text: Decompression sickness may occur as from :- 1: an altitude of more than 18,000 ft- 2 : an altitude of more than 5,500 ft- 3 : a rate of climb of more than 500 ft/min exceeding 18,000 ft- 4 : a temperature of more than 24°C
explanation: Decompression sickness typically becomes a hazard during flight at altitudes above 18,000 feet, or during rapid climbs to these altitudes where dissolved nitrogen begins to form bubbles in blood and tissues.

question_text: With regard to decompression sickness associated with flight, we know that :
option_a: age, obesity and scuba diving are risk factors
option_b: scuba diving does not pose any problem for a subsequent flight
option_c: sex is the prime risk factor, with two out of every three women being sensitive to it
option_d: physical activity after decompression reduces the risks of decompression sickness symptoms to appear
explanation: Risk factors that increase susceptibility to altitude decompression sickness include advanced age, obesity (as nitrogen is highly soluble in fat tissue), and recent SCUBA diving activity.

question_text: The procedure to be followed in the event of decompression when flying above 10,000 ft must :
option_a: allow for the rapid supply of oxygen in order to prevent the pilot becoming hypoxic
option_b: allow for a rapid descent independent from sufficient supply of oxygen in order to prevent disorders due to hypoxia
option_c: make it possible to prevent hyperventilation owing to the inhalation of 100 % oxygen
option_d: make it possible to eliminate the risk of fogging due to the sudden pressure changes
explanation: The emergency procedures for cabin decompression prioritize the immediate use of supplemental oxygen to prevent the crew from becoming hypoxic and incapacitated before starting a rapid descent.

question_text: What is the ""Time of Useful Consciousness"" for a rapid decompression at 25,000 ft ?
option_a: Between 3 and 5 minutes depending on the physical activities of the subjected pilot
explanation: At 25,000 feet, the Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) is typically between 3 and 5 minutes, although it can be significantly shorter if the pilot is engaged in physical activity.

question_text: A passenger complains about a painful inflated belly at 8.000 feet. You advise him to:1. unbuckle and massage the belly2. stand up and let go the gases out of the intestines3. eat less gas forming food and avoid carbonhydrated beverages before flight in the future4. drink a lot of water throughout the flight
option_a: 1, 2 and 3 are correct
explanation: To relieve the discomfort of expanding intestinal gas at altitude, passengers should massage the abdomen, stand up to pass gas, and avoid carbonated drinks or gas-forming foods before flight.

question_text: On ascent the gases in the digestive tract will
option_a: expand
option_d: be absorbed by tissues and blood
explanation: In accordance with Boyle's Law, gas trapped in the digestive tract will expand as the aircraft climbs and the ambient atmospheric pressure decreases.

question_text: Pain in the middle ear during descent may be eased by:
option_a: leveling off and possibly climbing
option_b: blocking the effected ear with the palm of your hand
explanation: Middle ear pain during descent is caused by negative pressure relative to the outside. Leveling off or climbing reduces this pressure differential, allowing the Eustachian tube to open and equalize the ear.

question_text: The Time of Useful Consciousness may vary according to :1 : physical activity of the subjected crew2 : the experience of the pilot on the type of aircraft in question3 : the strength and time of decompression4 : the cabin temperature
explanation: The Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) varies based on the level of physical exertion (which increases oxygen consumption) and the rate and magnitude of the cabin decompression.

question_text: During a climb, we can observe the following with regard to the partial oxygen pressure :
option_a: an identical decrease to that for atmospheric pressure
option_b: a decrease which is three times faster than the decrease in atmospheric pressure
option_c: an increase up to 10,000 ft followed by a sudden pressure drop above that altitude
option_d: an increase which is inversely proportional to the decrease in atmospheric pressure
