explanation: Accelerating or decelerating in level flight shifts the otolith organs, causing the brain to misinterpret the forces as pitching up (climbing) or pitching down (descending), respectively.

question_text: To prevent vertigo in flight we should
option_a: not move the head suddenly while we are turning
option_b: look towards the sides when we make a turn
option_c: breath deeply but control the respiratory frequency
explanation: To prevent spatial disorientation (vertigo) in flight, pilots should avoid making sudden, rapid head movements, especially while the aircraft is turning.

question_text: When stopping the rotation of a spin we have the sensation
option_a: that we are starting a spin into the opposite direction
option_b: of turning in the same direction
option_c: of the sharp dipping of the nose of the aircraft
option_d: of the immediate stabilization of the aircraft
explanation: Decelerating to recover from a spin stops the rotational movement of the canal walls, causing the endolymph to flow forward and bend the cupula, creating the false sensation of starting a spin in the opposite direction.

question_text: When accelerating in level flight we could experience the sensation of a
option_a: climb
explanation: When an aircraft accelerates forward in level flight, the inertial force slides the otoliths backward, creating a somatogravic illusion of pitching up or climbing.

question_text: During flight in IMC, the most reliable sense which should be used to overcome illusions is the:
option_a: visual sense, interpreting the attitude indicator
explanation: In instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), the visual interpretation of the attitude indicator is the only reliable sensory input available to maintain spatial orientation.

question_text: Spatial disorientation will be most likely to occur during flight:
option_a: if the brain receives conflicting informations and the pilot does not believe the instruments
option_b: when flying in and out of clouds and the pilot maintains good instrument cross check
option_c: when flying in light rain below the ceiling
option_d: when flying in bright sunlight above a cloud layer
explanation: Spatial disorientation is highly likely to occur when the brain receives conflicting signals from the eyes and vestibular system, and the pilot fails to trust the flight instruments.

question_text: Autokinetic illusion is:
option_a: an illusion in which a stationary point of light, if stared at for several seconds in the dark, may - without a frame of reference - appear to move
option_b: the sensation during a radial acceleration of seeing a fixed reference point moving into the opposite direction of the acceleration
option_c: a conflict between the visual system and bodily sensations
option_d: poor interpretation of the surrounding world
explanation: The autokinetic illusion occurs when a pilot stares at an isolated, stationary light source in the dark, which then appears to drift or move due to a lack of visual frames of reference.

question_text: With regard to illusions due to perceptive conflicts, it may be said that they:
option_a: are mainly due to a sensory conflict concerning perception of the vertical and the horizontal between the vestibular and the visual system
option_b: originate from a conflict between instrument readings and external visual perceptions
option_c: are caused by the absence of internal visual cues exclusively
option_d: are caused by a conflictual disagreement concerning attitudinal perception between the various members of a crew
explanation: Visual illusions in aviation are primarily caused by sensory conflicts between the visual system and the vestibular system regarding the perception of the true vertical and horizontal.

question_text: Visual disturbances can be caused by:1. hyperventilation2. hypoxia3. hypertension4. fatigue
option_a: 1, 2 and 4 are correct
explanation: Acute visual disturbances in flight can be caused by the physiological stressors of hypoxic hypoxia, hyperventilation, and extreme fatigue.

question_text: Desorientation is more likely to occur when the pilot is:1. flying in IMC2. frequently changing between inside and outside references3. flying from IMC into VMC4. having a cold
option_a: 1, 2 and 4 are correct
explanation: Spatial disorientation is more likely to occur when flying in IMC, when frequently switching between cockpit instruments and outside references, or when a cold blocks middle ear equalization.

question_text: Positive linear accelleration when flying in IMC may cause a false sensation of:
option_a: pitching up
option_c: apparent sideward movement of objects in the field of vision
explanation: Positive linear acceleration in IMC stimulates the otolith organs, which the brain misinterprets as a change in gravity direction, creating a somatogravic illusion of pitching up.

question_text: Linear accelleration when flying straight and level in IMC may give the illusion of:
option_a: climbing
explanation: Linear acceleration during straight-and-level flight in IMC acts on the utricle and saccule, generating a somatogravic illusion that the aircraft is climbing.

question_text: Coriolis illusion, causing spatial disorientation is the result of:
option_a: simultaneous head movements during aircraft manoeuvres
option_c: gazing in the direction of a flashing light
option_d: normal deterioration of the semicircular canals with age
explanation: The Coriolis illusion is a highly disorienting vestibular error resulting from making simultaneous head movements in a different plane than the aircraft's ongoing rotational maneuver.

question_text: When turning in IMC , head movements should be avoided as much as possible. This is a prevention against:
option_a: coriolis illusion
explanation: To prevent the Coriolis illusion, pilots must avoid moving their heads suddenly or looking down to adjust radios while the aircraft is turning in IMC.

question_text: Which of the following illusions are brought about by conflicts between the visual system and the vestibular system ?-1: Illusions concerning the attitude of the aircraft-2: Autokinetic illusion (fixed point viewed as moving)-3: Illusions when estimating the size and distance of objects-4 : Illusions of rotation
explanation: Conflicts between the visual and vestibular systems primarily produce spatial illusions regarding the attitude of the aircraft and false sensations of rotation.

question_text: A pilot, trying to pick up a fallen object from the cockpit floor during a tight turn, experiences:
option_a: coriolis illusion
explanation: A pilot who bends down to pick up a map or object from the cockpit floor during a tight turn is highly susceptible to the Coriolis illusion and severe vertigo.

question_text: When a pilot is starring at an isolated stationary light for several seconds in the dark he might get the illusion that:
option_a: the light is moving
option_b: the size of the lightis varying
option_c: the intensity of the light is varying
option_d: the colour of the light is varying
explanation: Staring continuously at a single, stationary light source in the dark for a few seconds can create the autokinetic illusion, where the light appears to move.

question_text: When you stare at a single light against the dark (f.e. an isolated star) you will find the light appears to move after some time. This phenomenon is called:
option_a: autokinetic phenomenon
explanation: The autokinetic phenomenon is a visual illusion where a single, isolated light in the dark appears to move or drift when stared at continuously.

question_text: How is haze effecting your perception?
option_a: Objects seem to be further away than in reality.
option_c: Haze makes the eyes to focus at infinity
option_d: Objects seem to be closer than in reality.
explanation: Haze reduces visual contrast and detail, causing the brain's aerial perspective cues to misinterpret the runway or terrain as being farther away than it actually is.

question_text: The 'Black hole' phenomenon occurs during approaches at night and over water, jungle or desert. When the pilot is lacking of visual cues other than those of the aerodrome there is an illusion of
option_a: being too high and too far away, dropping low and landing short
option_d: being too low, flying a steeper approach than normal
explanation: The 'black hole' phenomenon occurs during night approaches over dark terrain or water where the lack of peripheral visual cues causes the pilot to feel too high, leading to a low approach and short landing.

question_text: You fly VFR from your home base (runway width 27 m), to an international airport (runway width 45 m). On reaching your destination there is a risk of performing a:
option_a: high approach with overshoot
explanation: Flying from a home base with a 27-meter wide runway to land on a 45-meter wide runway will make the runway appear closer and lower than normal. The pilot may fly a high approach, risking an overshoot.

question_text: You fly VFR from your home base (runway width 45 m) to a small airfield (runway width 27 m). On reaching your destination there is a risk of performing a:
option_a: low approach with undershoot
explanation: Transitioning from a 45-meter wide runway to a narrower 27-meter wide runway makes the runway appear farther away and higher. The pilot may fly a low approach, risking an undershoot.

question_text: 1. In case of conflicting information you can always trust your Seat- of-the-Pants- Sense.2. In case of conflicting information between the sensory organs and the instruments you must believe the instruments.
option_a: 1 is false, 2 is correct
explanation: The proprioceptive ('seat-of-the-pants') sense is completely unreliable in IMC, meaning pilots must always trust the flight instruments in the event of sensory conflicts.

question_text: How can spatial disorientation in IMC be avoided? By
option_a: maintaining a good instrument cross check.
option_c: moving the head into the direction of the resultant vertical.
option_d: looking outside whenever possible ignoring the attitude indicator.
explanation: Spatial disorientation in IMC can be avoided by maintaining a disciplined, continuous instrument cross-check and relying entirely on instrument indications rather than physical sensations.

question_text: Which procedure is recommended to prevent or overcome spatial disorientation?
option_a: Rely entirely on the indications of the flight instruments.
option_b: Tilt your head to the side to get better informations from the semicircular canals.
option_d: Get adapted to low levels of illumination before flying and use off-center vision all the time.
explanation: To prevent or overcome spatial disorientation, a pilot must disregard all bodily sensations ('seat-of-the-pants' cues) and rely exclusively on the flight instruments.

question_text: How can a pilot prevent spatial disorientation in flight?
option_a: Establish and maintain a good instrument cross check.
option_b: Always try to catch outside visual cues.
option_c: Rely on good situational awareness believing your natural senses.
explanation: Pilots can prevent spatial disorientation in flight by establishing a disciplined instrument scan and ignoring vestibular and proprioceptive illusions that conflict with instrument readings.

question_text: If you are subjected to an illusion during night flying you should:
option_a: continue on instruments
explanation: If a pilot experiences a visual or vestibular illusion during night flying, they must immediately suppress their physical feelings and continue flying solely by reference to the flight instruments.

question_text: If you are disorientated during night flying you must:
option_a: relay on instruments
option_d: check your rate of breathing - do not breathe too fast
explanation: If disoriented during a night flight, the pilot's primary and immediate response must be to trust and rely on the cockpit flight instruments.

question_text: Which of the following statements are correct ?1 Hypothermia affects physical and mental abilities.2 Man has effective natural protection against intense cold.3 Shivering makes it possible to combat the cold to a certain extent, but uses up a lot of energy4 Disorders associated with hypothermia appear at a body temperature of less than 35°C
explanation: Hypothermia degrades physical coordination and cognitive functions. While shivering generates heat at a high energy cost, human core temperature below 35°C leads to clinical apathy and confusion.

question_text: Our body takes its energy from :1: minerals2: protein3: carbonhydrates4: vitamines
explanation: The human body obtains its metabolic energy from carbohydrates and proteins (macronutrients), whereas vitamins and minerals are micronutrients that do not provide caloric energy.

question_text: Which of the following mechanisms regulate body temperature when expored to extreme high environmental temperatures?-1 : Shivering-2 : Vasoconstriction of peripheral blood vessels-3 : Sweating-4 : Vasodilation of peripheral blood vessels
explanation: When exposed to high environmental temperatures, the body maintains its core temperature through peripheral vasodilation (bringing blood to the skin to dissipate heat) and sweating (evaporative cooling).

question_text: The following can be observed when the internal body temperature falls below 35°C :
option_a: shivering, will tend to cease, and be followed by the onset of apathy
explanation: When the internal body temperature drops below 35°C, physiological defense mechanisms begin to fail; shivering tends to cease and is replaced by apathy, muscle stiffness, and cognitive decline.

question_text: We can observe the following in relation to a state of hypothermia :
option_a: reasoning problems as soon as body temperature falls below 37°C
option_b: a substantial increase in internal body temperature whereas peripheral temperature at the skin is stable
option_c: a rapid fall in ambient temperature
option_d: greater capacity for adaptation than in a hot atmosphere
explanation: During hypothermia, core body temperature falls, leading to cognitive impairment, reasoning difficulties, and slowed reaction times as soon as temperature starts to drop below the normal 37°C baseline.

question_text: What is meant by metabolism ?
option_a: The transformation by which energy is made available for the uses of the organism
option_d: Exchange of substances between the lung and the blood
explanation: Metabolism refers to the chemical processes within a living organism by which food substances are broken down and transformed to make energy available for cellular activity and survival.

question_text: One of the waste products of the metabolic process in the cell is :
option_a: water
explanation: Water is a major chemical waste product of the cellular metabolic process (along with carbon dioxide), resulting from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

question_text: The body loses water via:1. the skin and the lungs2. the kidneys
option_a: 1 and 2 are correct
option_b: 1 is correct and 2 is not correct
option_c: 1 is not correct and 2 is correct
explanation: The human body continuously loses water through insensible dissipation via the skin and lungs (exhalation), as well as through active excretion by the kidneys.

question_text: It is inadvisable to fly when suffering from a cold. The reason for this is:
option_a: pain and damage to the eardrum can result, particularly during fast descents
option_b: gentle descents at high altitude can result in damage to the ear drum
option_c: swollen tissue in the inner ear will prevent the air from ventilating through the tympanic membrane
option_d: swollen tissue in the Eustachian tube will cause permanent hearing loss
explanation: Flying with a cold is dangerous because swollen tissues can block the Eustachian tube, preventing middle ear pressure equalization and causing severe pain or eardrum rupture during rapid descents.

question_text: It is inadvisable to fly when suffering from a cold. The reason for this is:
option_a: the tissue around the nasal end of the Eustachian tube is likely to be swollen thus causing difficulty in equalising the pressure within the middle ear and the nasal/throat area. Pain and damage to the eardrum can result, particularly during fast descents
option_b: although the change in air pressure during a climb at lower altitudes is very small, it increases rapidly at high altitudes. If the tissue in the Eustachian tube of the ear is swollen, gentle descents at high alltitude would result in damage to the ear drum
option_c: swollen tissue in the inner ear will increase the rate of metabolic production resulting in hyperventilation
option_d: because it will seriously affect peripheral vision
explanation: A cold causes inflammation and swelling of the nasal end of the Eustachian tube. This prevents pressure equalization between the middle ear and throat, leading to barotrauma and severe pain during descent.

question_text: Exchange of gasses between the body and the environment takes place at the:
option_a: lungs
explanation: External respiration, which is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide gases between the body and the ambient environment, takes place across the thin alveolar membranes in the lungs.

question_text: The following occurs in man if the internal body temperature increases to 38°C :
option_a: impairment of physical and mental performance
option_d: nothing signifiant happens at this temperature. The first clinical signs only start to appear at 39°C
explanation: An increase in core body temperature to 38°C (mild hyperthermia) causes early impairment of physical coordination and cognitive performance, reducing situational awareness.

question_text: Having a serious cold it is better not to fly, due to the extra risk of:1. flatulence2. pain in the ear during descent3. pressure vertigo4. pain in the nasal sinuses
option_a: 2,3 and 4 are correct
explanation: Flying with a serious cold increases the risk of middle ear barotrauma (ear pain), pressure vertigo (due to asymmetric pressure equalization), and sinus barotrauma (sinus pain).

question_text: Having a serious cold, you are going to fly. What can you expect:
option_a: pain in the sinuses
explanation: If a pilot flies with a serious cold, the inability to equalize air pressure in the sinuses and middle ear cavities can result in severe localized facial and ear pain.

question_text: Which of the following factors may have an influence on medical disqualification?
option_a: High and low blood pressure as well as a poor condition of the circulatory system.
option_c: Blood pressure problems cannot occur in aircrew because they always can be treated by in- flight medication.
explanation: Both high and low blood pressure, along with overall deficiencies in the cardiovascular system, are significant factors that can lead to medical disqualification for flight crew.

question_text: When assessing an individuals risk in developing coronary artery disease, the following factors may contribute:1.obesity2.distress3.smoking4.family history
option_a: 1, 2, 3 and 4 are correct
option_b: 2 and 3 are correct, 1 and 4 are false
option_c: Only 3 is correct, 1, 2 and 4 are false
explanation: The risk of developing coronary artery disease is increased by a combination of lifestyle and genetic factors, including obesity, chronic distress, tobacco smoking, and a family history of heart disease.

question_text: Noise induced hearing loss is influenced by
option_a: the duration and intensity of a noise
option_b: the duration of a noise but not its intensity
option_c: the suddenness of onset of a noise
option_d: the intensity of the noise but not its duration
explanation: The severity of noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is directly determined by both the duration of exposure and the physical intensity (decibel level) of the noise.

question_text: To reduce the risk of coronary artery disease, exercise should be
option_a: double the resting heart rate for at least 20 minutes, three times a week
option_b: avoided since raising the heart rate shortens the life of the heart
option_c: double the resting heart rate for at least an hour, five times a week
option_d: triple the resting heart rate for 20 minutes, once a week
explanation: To maintain cardiovascular health and reduce coronary risk, aerobic exercise should raise the heart rate to approximately double its resting rate for at least 20 minutes, three times a week.

question_text: Which of the following is most true?
option_a: Regular exercise is beneficial to general health, but the most efficient way to lose weight is by reducing caloric consumption
option_b: Regular exercise is an impediment to losing weight since it increases the metabolic rate
option_c: Regular exercise is beneficial to general health, and is the only effective way to lose weight
option_d: Regular exercise and reduction in caloric consumption are both essential in order to lose weight
explanation: Regular exercise is highly beneficial for cardiovascular health and general fitness, but reducing daily caloric consumption remains the most efficient method for achieving weight loss.

question_text: Conductive hearing loss can be caused by: 1. damage to the ossicles in the middle ear caused by infection or trauma 2. a damage of the auditory nerve 3. an obstruction in the auditory duct 4. a ruptured tympanic membrane
option_a: 1,2,3 and 4 are correct
explanation: Conductive hearing loss is caused by mechanical blockages in sound transmission, such as damage to the ossicles, an obstruction in the auditory canal, or a ruptured eardrum.

question_text: Noise induced hearing loss (NIHL) is caused by:
option_a: damage of the sensitive membrane in the cochlea due to overexposure to noise
option_c: pressure differences on both sides of the eardrum
explanation: Noise-induced hearing loss is a sensorineural impairment caused by damage to the delicate sensory hair cells on the basilar membrane within the cochlea due to overexposure to high noise levels.

question_text: Which of the following statements about hyperthermia is correct ?
option_a: Complete adaption to the heat in a hot country takes about a fortnight.
option_b: Vasodilation is the only regulant which is capable of reducing body temperature.
option_c: Evaporation is more effective when ambient humidity is high.
option_d: Performance is not impaired by an increase in body temperature to 40°C or more.
explanation: Acclimatization to a hot climate involves progressive physiological adjustments (like increased sweat rate) and typically requires about two weeks (a fortnight) of gradual exposure.

question_text: Visual acuity during flight at high altitudes can be affected by: 1. anaemia 2. smoking in the cockpit 3. carbon monoxide poisoning 4. hypoxia
option_a: 1, 2, 3 and 4 are correct
explanation: Visual acuity and night vision can be significantly degraded at high altitudes by factors that reduce retinal oxygenation, including anaemia, smoking, carbon monoxide poisoning, and hypoxic hypoxia.

question_text: Alcohol, even when taken in minor quantities
option_a: can make the brain cells to be more susceptible to hypoxia
option_b: will stimulate the brain, making the pilot resistant to hypoxia
option_c: will have no effect at all
option_d: may improve the mental functions, so that the symptoms of hypoxia are much better to be identified
explanation: Alcohol, even in small quantities, acts as a cellular toxin that interferes with cellular oxidation, making brain cells significantly more susceptible to the effects of hypoxia.

question_text: Concerning flying and blood alcohol content the following statement is correct:
option_a: no flying under the influence of alcohol
option_b: flying with up to 0.05 % blood alcohol
option_c: flying with up to 0.15 % blood alcohol
option_d: flying with up to 0.08 % blood alcohol is safe, since driving is safe up to this limit
explanation: Aviation safety standards maintain a strict rule that pilots must not operate an aircraft while under the influence of alcohol, emphasizing a zero-tolerance approach.

question_text: The metabolisation of alcohol
option_a: is a question of time
option_b: is quicker when used to it
option_c: can be accelerated even more by coffee
option_d: can be influenced by easy to get medication
explanation: The liver metabolizes and eliminates alcohol from the bloodstream at a constant, slow rate that is strictly a function of time and cannot be accelerated by stimulants or remedies.

question_text: Concerning the effects of drugs and pilot´s performance
option_a: the primary and the side effects have to be considered
option_b: the side effects only have to be considered
option_c: medication has no influence on pilot´s performance
option_d: only the primary effect has to be considered, side effects are negligable
explanation: When evaluating a pilot's fitness to fly while taking medication, both the primary therapeutic effects and the potential adverse side effects of the drug must be carefully analyzed.

question_text: Drugs against allergies (antihistamines), when taken by an aviator can cause the following undesirable effects:1. Drowsiness, dizziness2. Dry mouth3. Headaches4. Impaired depth perception5. Nausea
option_a: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are correct
explanation: Antihistamines commonly used to treat allergies can cause undesirable side effects in aviators, including drowsiness, dry mouth, headache, nausea, and impaired depth perception.

question_text: The consumption of medicines or other substances may have consequences on qualification to fly for the following reasons:1. The desease requiring a treatment may be cause for disqualification.2. Flight conditions may modify the reactions of the body to a treatment.3. Drugs may cause adverse side effects impairing flight safety.4. The effects of medicine do not necessarily immediately disappear when the treatment is stopped.
option_a: 1, 2, 3 and 4 are correct
option_c: 3 and 4 are false, 1 and 2 are correct.
explanation: The use of medications can disqualify a pilot because the underlying illness may be unsafe, flight conditions can alter drug reactions, side effects can impair safety, and drug clearance takes time.

question_text: Cigarette smoking has particular significance to the flyer, because there are long- term and short-term harmful effects. From cigarette smoking the pilot can get:
option_a: a mild carbon monoxide poisoning decreasing the pilot´s tolerance to hypoxia
option_b: a mild carbon dioxide poisoning increasing the pilot's tolerance to hypoxia
option_c: a mild carbon monoxide poisoning increasing the pilot´s tolerance to hypoxia
option_d: a suppressed desire to eat and drink
explanation: Tobacco smoking introduces carbon monoxide into the bloodstream, where it binds to hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport and lowering the pilot's tolerance to hypoxia.

question_text: A pilot who smokes will loose some of his capacity to transport oxygen combined with hemoglobin. Which percentage of his total oxygen transportation capacity would he give away when he smokes one pack of cigarettes a day?
explanation: A pilot who smokes a pack of cigarettes a day typically has 5% to 8% of their total hemoglobin bound by carbon monoxide, representing a significant loss in oxygen-carrying capacity.

question_text: Flying at pressure altitude of 10 000 ft, a pilot, being a moderate to heavy smoker, has an oxygen content in the blood equal to an altitude
option_a: above 10 000 FT
explanation: Due to the presence of carbon monoxide in their blood, a moderate to heavy smoker has a reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, elevating their physiological altitude above their actual cabin pressure altitude.

question_text: Which of the following applies when alcohol has been consumed?
option_a: Even after the consumption of small amounts of alcohol, normal cautionary attitudes may be lost
option_b: Drinking coffee at the same time will increase the elimination rate of alcohol
option_c: Small amounts of alcohol increase visual performance
option_d: Acute effects of alcohol cease immediately when 100% oxygen is taken
explanation: Alcohol consumption degrades judgment and risk perception, causing pilots to lose their normal cautionary attitudes and engage in risky behavior even after consuming small amounts.

question_text: Alcohol, when taken simultaneously with drugs, may
option_a: intensify the effects of the drugs
option_b: compensate for side effects of drugs
option_c: show undesired effects only during night flights
option_d: increase the rate of alcohol elimination from the blood
explanation: Taking alcohol simultaneously with other medications can produce synergistic interactions, dramatically intensifying the sedating and impairing side effects of the drugs.

question_text: Alcohol metabolism (elimination rate)
option_a: is approx. 0.015% per hour and cannot be expedited
option_c: depends on wether you get some sleep in between drinks
option_d: definitely depends on the amount and composition of food which has been eaten
explanation: The human liver metabolizes alcohol at a constant rate of approximately 0.015% blood alcohol concentration (BAC) per hour, a biochemical process that cannot be accelerated.

question_text: When drugs against sleep disorders and/or nervosity have been taken and the pilot intends to fly, attention has to be payed to
option_a: the effect they have on reaction time and perceptional awareness
option_b: the effect they have on hearing
option_c: the fact that there is no difference in the quality of sleep produced under the influence of those drugs compared to normal drug-free sleep
option_d: schedule only those pilots, who show no reactions to these medications
explanation: Pilots must avoid flying under the influence of sedatives or sleep medications because these drugs impair motor reaction times, vigilance, and overall perceptual awareness.

question_text: The rate of absorption of alcohol depends on many factors. However, the rate of metabolism or digestion of alcohol in the body is relatively constant. It is about
option_a: 0,01 - 0,015 mg % per hour
explanation: The rate at which the body metabolizes alcohol is constant and slow, averaging approximately 0.01% to 0.015% (or equivalent mg% units) per hour, regardless of food or caffeine intake.

question_text: A slight lack of coordination which can make it difficult to carry out delicate and precise movements occurs when the level of alcohol in the blood is exceeding
option_a: 0.05 % blood alcohol
explanation: A blood alcohol concentration exceeding 0.05% causes a measurable degradation in motor coordination, reaction times, and the ability to execute precise cockpit control movements.

question_text: The carcinogen (a substance with the ability to produce modifications in cells which develop a cancer) in the bronchi of the lungs is
option_a: tar
explanation: Tar is the primary carcinogen present in cigarette smoke, depositing in the bronchi and lungs where it damages cells and promotes the development of lung cancer.

question_text: One of the substances present in the smoke of cigarettes can make it significantly more difficult for the red blood cells to transport oxygen and as a consequence contributes to hypoxia. Which substance are we referring to?
option_a: Carbon monoxide
explanation: Carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke binds to hemoglobin with an affinity 200 times greater than oxygen, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and contributing to hypemic hypoxia.

question_text: The so-called Coriolis effect (a conflict in information processing in the brain) in spatial disorientation occurs:
option_a: on stimulating several semicircular canals simultaneously
option_b: on stimulating the saccule and the utricle of the inner ear
option_d: when no semicircular canal is stimulated
explanation: The Coriolis illusion is a highly disorienting vestibular illusion that occurs when a pilot moves their head out of the plane of rotation, stimulating multiple semicircular canals simultaneously.

question_text: The chemical substance responsible for addiction to tobacco is
option_a: nicotine
option_d: the combination of nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide
explanation: Nicotine is the highly addictive chemical substance present in tobacco that drives physical dependence and makes smoking cessation difficult.

question_text: A large number of medical preparations can be bought without a doctor´s prescription. In relation to using these preparations, which of the following is correct:
option_a: A pilot using any of these preparations should get professional advice from a flight surgeon if he intends to fly and self-medicate at the same time
option_b: They have no side effects which would give problems to a pilot during flight
option_c: The side effects of these types of preparations are sufficiently negligible as to be ignored by pilots
option_d: They will cause a condition of over-arousal
explanation: Self-medication with over-the-counter drugs is hazardous for pilots; they must always consult a flight surgeon to ensure the medication has no side effects that compromise flight safety.

question_text: Carbon monoxide, a product of incomplete combustion, is toxic because
option_a: it competes with oxygen in its union with haemoglobin
option_b: it prevents the absorption of food from the digestive tract
option_c: it prevents the excretion of catabolites in the kidneys
option_d: it disturbs gaseous diffusion at the alveoli capillary membrane
explanation: Carbon monoxide is highly toxic because it actively competes with oxygen for binding sites on the hemoglobin molecule, forming a stable compound that prevents oxygen transport.

question_text: Carbon monoxide is always present in the exhaust gases of engines. If a pilot is exposed to carbon monoxide, which of the following responses is correct?
option_a: A short exposure to relatively high concentrations of carbon monoxide can seriously affect a pilot´s ability to operate an aircraft.
option_b: Carbon monoxide is easily recognised by odour and taste.
option_c: Carbon monoxide can only affect pilots if they are exposed to them for a long period of time.
option_d: When exposed to carbon monoxide for a long period of time, the body will adapt to it and no adverse physical effects are experienced
explanation: Engine exhaust contains carbon monoxide. Inhaling even low concentrations of this odorless, tasteless gas can rapidly impair a pilot's cognitive abilities, judgment, and motor control.

question_text: Adverse effects of carbon monoxide increase as:
option_a: altitude increases
explanation: As altitude increases, the lower partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere compounds the effects of carbon monoxide poisoning, causing symptoms to develop faster and become more severe.

question_text: Which statement is correct regarding alcohol in the human body?
option_a: Judgement and decision making can be affected even by a small amount of alcohol.
option_b: A small amount of alcohol increases visual acuity.
option_c: An increase of altitude decreases the adverse effect of alcohol.
option_d: When drinking coffee, the human body metabolizes alcohol at a faster rate than normal.
explanation: Even small amounts of alcohol can significantly degrade cognitive judgment and decision-making capabilities, which is highly dangerous in aviation where blood-alcohol limits are strictly regulated.

question_text: Which statement is correct? 1. Smokers have a greater chance of suffering from coronary heart disease 2. Smoking tobacco will raise the individuals pysiological altitude during flight3. Smokers have a greater chance of decreasing ung cancer
option_a: 1,2 and 3 are correct
explanation: Smoking tobacco introduces carbon monoxide into the bloodstream, which raises a pilot's physiological altitude. It also significantly increases the risk of developing coronary heart disease and lung cancer.

question_text: Smoking cigarettes reduces the capability of the blood to carry oxygen. This is because:
option_a: hemoglobin has a greater affinity for carbon monoxide than it has for oxygen
option_b: carbon monoxide in the smoke of cigarettes assists diffusion of oxygen in the alveoli
option_c: carbon monoxide increases the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli
option_d: the smoke of one cigarette can cause an obstruction in the respiratory tract
explanation: Cigarette smoke contains carbon monoxide, which binds to hemoglobin with an affinity approximately 200 times greater than oxygen, reducing the blood's capacity to transport oxygen to body tissues.

question_text: CO (carbon monoxide) present in the smoke of cigarettes can lead to: 1. reduction of time of usefull consciousness 2. hypoxia at a much lower altitude than normal
option_a: 1 and 2 are both correct
explanation: Carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke binds to hemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. This can lead to a shorter Time of Useful Consciousness and the onset of hypoxia at much lower altitudes.

question_text: Carbon monoxide in the human body can lead to: 1. loss of muscular power2. headache 3. impaired judgement 4. pain in the joints 5. loss of consciousness
option_a: 1, 2 , 3 and 5 are correct
explanation: Carbon monoxide poisoning leads to tissue hypoxia, which clinically manifests as headaches, muscle weakness, impaired judgment, confusion, and eventual loss of consciousness.

question_text: Incapacitation is most dangerous when it is :
option_a: insinuating
explanation: Insinuating (insidious) incapacitation is the most dangerous type because it is gradual and subtle, meaning the affected pilot may perform poorly or make errors without either crew member realizing it.

question_text: The human information processing system is highly efficient compared to computers because of its
option_a: flexibility
explanation: The human information processing system is highly superior to computers due to its flexibility, allowing pilots to improvise, recognize complex patterns, and adapt to novel or unexpected situations.

question_text: In an abnormal situation the pilot has an apparently correct explanation for the problem. The chance that he/she now ignores or devalues other relevant information, not fitting into his/her mental picture is:
option_a: increasing
option_b: the same, no matter if he/she has already made up his/her mind
option_c: not applicable with old and experienced pilots
explanation: Once a pilot has formed an initial mental model of a situation, confirmation bias increases. This causes them to actively search for or value confirming data while ignoring or devaluing contradictory information.

question_text: Many pilots think up systems to deal with affairs so they don't have to think up every time what they have to do.
option_a: this has to be posetively appreciated for it increases consistency in action
option_b: this is dangerous for every situation is different
option_c: this has to be rejected for the company draws the rules and the procedures they have to comply with
option_d: this has to be advised against for it reduces flexibility at a moment a problem has to be solved by improvisation.
explanation: Developing systematic personal routines and heuristics for cockpit operations is beneficial because it increases consistency in action, reduces cognitive load, and helps prevent simple slips and omissions.

question_text: Mental schemes correspond to:
option_a: memorised representations of the various procedures and situations which can be reactivated by the pilot at will
option_b: the memorisation of regulatory procedures associated with a particular situation
option_c: memorised procedures which develop and change rapidly during change-over to a new machine
option_d: daily planning of probable dangerous situations
explanation: Mental schemes are structured, memorized representations of various procedures and flight situations stored in long-term memory that can be rapidly retrieved and applied to guide actions.

question_text: The acquisition of expertise comprises three stages ( Anderson model):
option_a: cognitive, associative and autonomous
explanation: According to Anderson's model of skill acquisition, the three progressive stages of expertise development are the cognitive stage, the associative stage, and the autonomous stage.

question_text: A pilot can be described as being proficient, when he/she:
option_a: has automated a large part of the necessary flight deck routine operations in order to free his/her cognitive resources
option_b: is able to reduce his/her arousal to a low level during the entire flight
option_c: knows how to invest the maximum resources in the automation of tasks in real time
option_d: is capable of maintaining a high level of arousal during a great bulk of the flight
explanation: A proficient pilot is one who has automated a large portion of routine flight deck operations. This frees up limited cognitive resources to focus on decision-making, planning, and monitoring.

question_text: The ability of detecting relevant information which is not presented in an actively monitored input channel is known as
option_a: attention
explanation: Selective attention is the cognitive process that allows a pilot to detect and process relevant information from secondary sources even when they are not actively monitoring that input channel.

question_text: According to Wicken's theory, the human brain has:
option_a: different reservoirs of resources depending on whether one is in the information-gathering, information-processing or action phase
option_c: cognitive resources which are centered on action
option_d: processing capabilities which function at peak level when different tasks call for the same resources
explanation: Wickens' Multiple Resource Model suggests that the human brain has different reservoirs of cognitive resources divided by stages of processing, sensory modalities, and codes.

question_text: The available cognitive resources of the human brain:
option_a: are limited and make it impossible to perform two attentional tasks at the same time
option_b: are limited but make it possible to easily perform several tasks at the same time
option_d: allow for twin-tasks operation without any loss of effectiveness
explanation: The cognitive processing resources of the human brain are strictly limited, making it impossible to perform two complex, attention-demanding tasks simultaneously without a drop in performance.

question_text: Concentration is essential for pilots.
option_a: However, capacity of concentration is limited
option_b: It only takes a little willpower to increase one's capacity of concentration without limits
option_c: Vigilance is all that is required to be attentive
option_d: All intellectual processes, including very routined ones, make demands on resources and therefore on one's concentration
explanation: Concentration is a limited cognitive resource; pilots must manage their workload because sustained high concentration cannot be maintained indefinitely without fatigue and performance decline.

question_text: The 'cocktail party effect' is
option_a: the ability to pick up relevant information unintentionally
option_b: the ability to drink too much at social gathering
option_c: the tendency to believe information that reinforces our mental model of the world
option_d: the tendency not to perceive relevant information
explanation: The 'cocktail party effect' is the cognitive ability to filter out background noise while subconsciously monitoring it, allowing a pilot to immediately shift attention when a highly relevant cue is heard.

question_text: Which of the following tasks are possible to do simultaneously without mutual interference?
option_a: Maintain manual straight and level flight and solve a problem.
option_b: Listen attentively and solve a problem.
option_c: Talk and rehearse a frequency in working memory.
explanation: Simultaneous tasks can be performed without interference only if one of the tasks is highly automated (like maintaining manual straight-and-level flight) and uses different cognitive resources than the second task.

question_text: A selective attentional mechanism is required
option_a: because of the limited capacity of the central decision maker and working memory
option_b: because the capacity of the long term memory is limited
option_c: because of the limitations of the sense organs
option_d: because of limitations in our store of motor programmes
explanation: A selective attention mechanism is necessary because of the limited capacity of the human working memory and the central executive processor, which cannot handle all sensory inputs simultaneously.

question_text: If a pilot has to perform two tasks requiring the allocation of cognitive resources :
option_a: the sharing of resources causes performance on each task to be reduced
option_b: a person reaches his limits as from simultaneous tasks, and performance will then tail off
option_c: the only way of not seeing performance tail off is to switch to knowledge-based mode for the two tasks
option_d: the only way of not seeing performance tail off is to switch to rules-based mode for the two tasks
explanation: When a pilot attempts to perform two tasks that require active cognitive resources, the sharing of these limited resources leads to a reduction in performance on both tasks.

question_text: Which of the following are the most favourable solutions to manage phases of reduced or low vigilance (hypovigilance)?1. Healthy living2. Use of amphetamines3. Reducing the intensity of the light4. Organising periods of rest during the flight
explanation: The most effective ways to manage phases of low vigilance (hypovigilance) during long flights are maintaining a healthy lifestyle/rest cycle and organizing structured in-flight rest periods among the crew.

question_text: What are main signs indicating the loss of vigilance ?1. Decrease in sensory perception2. Increase in selective attention3. Sensation of muscular heaviness4. Decrease in complacency
explanation: A loss of vigilance is typically indicated by a general decrease in sensory perception, slowed reaction times, and physical sensations of muscular heaviness or fatigue.

question_text: What is ""divided attention""?
option_a: Alternative management of several matters of interest
option_b: Ease of concentrating on a particular objective
option_c: Difficulty of concentrating on a particular objective
option_d: The adverse effect of motivation which leads to one's attention being dispersed
explanation: Divided attention refers to the rapid, alternating switching of focus between multiple tasks or interests, as true parallel processing of attention-demanding tasks is not possible.

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning hypovigilance is correct ? Hypovigilance :
option_a: may occur at any moment of the flight
option_b: essentially occurs several minutes after the intense take-off phase
option_c: tends to occur at the end of the mission as a result of a relaxation in the operators' attention
explanation: Hypovigilance (reduced alertness) is a common fatigue state that can occur at any moment during a flight, particularly during monotonous cruise phases, regardless of the pilot's personality.

question_text: What are the main factors which bring about reduced or low vigilance (hypovigilance) ?1. The monotony of the task2. Tiredness,the need for sleep3. A lack of stimulation4. Excessive stress
explanation: Hypovigilance is primarily caused by task monotony, sleep deprivation or fatigue, and a lack of external sensory stimulation, rather than acute stress which usually raises arousal.

question_text: With regard to the level of automation of behaviours in the attention mechanism, we know that :
option_a: the more behaviour is automated, the less it requires conscious attention and thus the more it frees mental resources
option_b: the more behaviour is automated, the more it requires attention and the more it frees resources
option_c: the more behaviour is automated, the more it requires attention and the less it frees resources
option_d: the less behaviour is automated, the less it requires attention and the more it frees resources
explanation: Behavioral automation is beneficial because the more a skill is automated, the less conscious attention it requires. This frees up limited cognitive resources for higher-level tasks.

question_text: What are the various factors which guide attention ?1. The level of automation of behaviour2. Response time3. The salience of the information4. Expectations
explanation: Human attention is guided and directed by a combination of the level of behavioral automation, the sensory salience of new information, and the pilot's cognitive expectations.

question_text: Check the following statements:1. The first information received determines how subsequent information will be evaluated.2. If one has made up one's mind, contradictory information may not get the attention it really needs.3. With increasing stress, channelizing attention is limiting the flow of information to the central decision maker (CNS).
option_a: 1, 2 and 3 are correct
explanation: Anchoring bias causes initial information to disproportionately shape situational assessment, and confirmation bias can lead to ignoring contradictory evidence, especially under stress which narrows attention.

question_text: Conscious perception
option_a: is a mental process involving experience and expectations
option_b: relies upon the development of intuition
option_c: involves the transfer of information from the receptor to the brain only
option_d: relates to the correct recognition of colours
explanation: Conscious perception is not just the passive receipt of sensory signals; it is an active mental process where the brain interprets inputs based on past experiences and current expectations.

question_text: The first stage in the information process is
option_a: sensory stimulation
explanation: The human information processing cycle begins with sensory stimulation, where physical receptors (eyes, ears, skin) detect environmental energy before perception and selection occur.

question_text: Our mental model of the world is based
option_a: on both our past experiences and the sensory information we receive
option_b: entirely on the sensory information we receive
option_d: on both our past experiences and our motor programmes
explanation: A pilot's mental model of the aircraft and environment is constructed using a combination of incoming sensory information and retrieved past experiences stored in long-term memory.

question_text: What is the main adverse effect of expectations in the perception mechanism ?
option_a: Expectations often guide the focus of attention towards a particular aspect, while possible alternates are neglected
option_b: They always lead to routine errors
option_c: The unconscious mechanism of attention leads to focus on all relevant information
option_d: The attention area is enlarged, thus it will lead to an uncertainty in regard to necessary decisions
explanation: Expectations strongly shape perception, which can be hazardous when they channelize attention toward confirming a preconceived idea while causing the pilot to overlook alternative, contradictory data.

question_text: Which of the following provides the basis of all perceptions?
option_a: The intensity of the stimuli.
option_b: The aural or visual significance attributed in short term memory.
option_c: The aural or visual significance attributed in long term memory.
option_d: The seperation of figure and background.
explanation: The physical intensity of a sensory stimulus (crossing the absolute threshold) provides the fundamental basis for all subsequent neural perception and cognitive processing.

question_text: The ""gestalt laws ""formulates :
option_a: basic principles governing how objects are mentally organized and perceived
option_b: basic principles governing the relationship between stress and performance
option_c: basic principles governing the effects of habit and experience
option_d: basic principles regarding to the relationship between motivation and performance
explanation: Gestalt laws describe the basic organizational principles used by the human brain to group, structure, and interpret visual stimuli into coherent objects and patterns.

question_text: Illusions of interpretation (cognitive illusions) are :
option_a: associated with the task of mental construction of the environment
option_b: due mainly to a conflict between the various sensory systems
option_c: due mainly to a poor interpretation of instrumental data
option_d: solely induced in the absence of external reference points
explanation: Cognitive illusions are errors in interpretation where the brain incorrectly constructs a mental model of the surrounding environment despite receiving normal sensory inputs.

question_text: In the absence of external reference points, the sensation that the vehicle in which you sitting is moving when it is in fact the vehicle directly alongside which is moving is called :
option_a: illusion of relative movement
explanation: The illusion of relative movement (vection) occurs in a dark or featureless environment where the movement of an adjacent object (like another aircraft) is falsely perceived as movement of one's own vehicle.

question_text: The maximum number of unrelated items that can be stored in working memory is:
option_a: about 7 items
explanation: The typical capacity of human working memory is limited, allowing for the temporary storage of approximately 7 unrelated items (the Miller magic number of 7 ± 2).

question_text: The capacity of the short-term memory is
option_a: about 7 items
explanation: Short-term memory has a very restricted capacity, generally limited to holding about 7 chunks of information at any one time.

question_text: Information stays in the short-term memory
option_a: about 20 seconds
explanation: Without active cognitive rehearsal, information stored in short-term memory decays rapidly, typically disappearing within approximately 20 seconds.

question_text: Working memory :
option_a: is sensitive to interruptions which may erase all or some of its content
option_d: varies considerably in size between an expert pilot and a novice pilot
explanation: Working memory is highly vulnerable to interruptions and distractions, which can easily erase some or all of the temporarily stored data from conscious awareness.

question_text: Long-term memory is an essential component of the pilot's knowledge and expertise.
option_a: It is desirable to pre-activate knowledge stored in long-term memory to have it available when required
option_b: The capacity of long-term memory is limited
option_c: Long-term memory stores knowledge on a temporary basis
option_d: The recovery of information from long-term memory is immediate and easy
explanation: Long-term memory contains vast stores of knowledge. Pre-activating (priming) this knowledge before a high-workload phase reduces retrieval time and eases cognitive demand.

question_text: Motor programmes are:
option_a: stored routines that enable patterns of behaviour to be executed without continuous conscious control
option_b: rules that enable us to deal with novel situations
option_c: rules that enable us to deal with preconceived situations
option_d: stored routines that enable patterns of behaviour to be executed only under continuous conscious control
explanation: Motor programs are structured, pre-learned sequences of movement stored in long-term memory that can be executed automatically without requiring continuous conscious attention.

question_text: Working memory enables us, for example,
option_a: to remember a clearance long enough to write it down
option_b: to store a large amount of visual information for about 0.5 seconds
option_c: to ignore messages for other aircraft
explanation: Working memory serves as a mental workspace, enabling a pilot to temporarily retain information (such as an ATC clearance) long enough to record it or act upon it.

question_text: In the short-term-memory, information is stored for approximately
option_a: 20 seconds
explanation: Without rehearsal or active maintenance, information in the short-term memory decays and is lost after approximately 20 seconds.

question_text: The main limit(s) of long-term memory is (are):
option_a: Data retrieval as a result from a loss of access to the stored information
option_b: the quantity of data which may be stored
option_c: the instantaneous inputting in memory of all information collected during the day, which comes to saturate it
explanation: The primary limitation of long-term memory is not storage capacity, but rather retrieval failure, which occurs when a pilot loses the pathway to access the stored information.

question_text: What are the main limits of short-term memory ?It is :-1 : very sensitive to interruptions and interference-2 : difficult to access-3 : limited in size-4 : subject to a biochemical burn-in of information
explanation: Short-term memory limitations include its extreme sensitivity to interference or distraction, its small storage capacity, and the requirement for consolidation to transfer data to long-term memory.

question_text: Which of the following characteristics apply to short-term memory ?- 1 : It is limited in time and size- 2 : It is unlimited in time and limited in size- 3 : It is stable and insensitive to disturbances- 4 : It is limited in time and unlimited in size
explanation: Short-term memory is characterized by a strictly limited capacity and a short duration, functioning as a temporary buffer for immediate information processing.

question_text: With regard to short-term memory, we can say that :
option_a: it is made up of everyday information for immediate use, and is limited in its capacity for storing and retaining data
option_b: it is made up of everyday information for immediate use, and is limited in terms of the time for which it retains data but not in its storage capacity
option_c: it is a stable form of working memory, and thus not very sensitive to any disturbance
explanation: Short-term memory functions as a temporary workspace with a small capacity, and is highly sensitive to disruptions, distraction, and decay.

question_text: Which of the following statements about long-term memory are correct?-1: Information is stored there in the form of descriptive, rule-based and schematic knowledge.-2: The period of time for which information is retained is limited by the frequency with which this same information is used.-3: It processes information quickly and has an effective mode of access in real time.-4: Pre-activation of necessary knowledge will allow for a reduction in access time.
option_a: 1 and 4 are correct
explanation: Long-term memory stores descriptive, rule-based, and schematic knowledge. Pre-activating relevant knowledge before a critical phase reduces access and retrieval times.

question_text: To facilitate and reduce the time taken to access information in long-term memory, it is helpful to:
option_a: mentally rehearse information before it is needed
option_b: learn and store data in a logical and structured way
option_c: structure irrelevant information as much as possible before committing it to memory
option_d: avoid to rehearse information which we know we will need soon
explanation: To ease and speed up the retrieval of information from long-term memory, it is helpful to mentally rehearse the information shortly before it is required, pre-activating the cognitive pathways.

question_text: Concerning the capacity of the human long-term memory
option_a: its storage capacity is unlimited
option_b: it is structurally limited in terms of storage capacity, but unlimted in terms of storage time
option_c: it is structurally limited in terms of storage time but not in terms of capacity
option_d: its mode of storing information is passive, making memory searches effective
explanation: The storage capacity of human long-term memory is practically unlimited, allowing an individual to accumulate vast amounts of knowledge and experiences over their lifetime.

question_text: Young pilots or pilots with little experience of airplanes differ from experienced pilots in the following way :
option_a: unexperienced pilots refer to information more than experts when carrying out the same task
option_b: experienced pilots are less routine-minded than young pilots because they know that routine causes mistakes
option_c: task for task, an expert's workload is greater than a novice's one
option_d: flight planning performance decreases with age, and experience is unable to mask this deficiency
explanation: Inexperienced pilots lack automated mental schemas, meaning they must refer to checklists and external information sources much more frequently than experts when executing the same tasks.

question_text: In order to provide optimum human performance it is advisable to
option_a: establish strategies for planning, automating and managing resources (in real time)
option_b: plan a maximum of objectives and non-automated actions
option_c: avoid powerful behaviour expedient of automating tasks
option_d: plan future actions and decisions at least a couple of days in advance
explanation: To optimize performance, flight crew must employ strategies for advance flight planning, task automation, and real-time resource management to prevent cognitive overload.

question_text: The planning and anticipation of future actions and situations makes it possible to:-1 : create a precise reference framework.-2 : avoid saturation of the cognitive system.-3 : automate planned actions.-4 : activate knowledge which is considered necessary for the period to come.The correct statement(s) is (are):
option_a: 1, 2 and 4 are correct
explanation: Anticipation and planning provide a precise reference framework, prevent cognitive saturation during high-workload phases, and pre-activate the knowledge needed for upcoming flight segments.

question_text: Pre-thought action plans may be said to:-1 : ease access to information which may be necessary.-2 : sensitize and prepare for a possible situation to come.-3 : be readily interchangeable and can therefore be reformulated at any time during the flight.-4 : define a framework and a probable strategy for the encountered situation.The combination of correct statements is:
option_a: 1, 2 and 4 are correct
explanation: Pre-thought action plans reduce cognitive workload, prepare the pilot for anticipated challenges, and establish a structured strategy for managing various flight phases.

question_text: The workload may be said to:-1 : be acceptable if it requires more than 90 % of the crew resources.-2 : be acceptable if it requires about 60 % of the crew resources.-3 : depend on the pilot's expertise.-4 : correspond to the amount of resources availableThe combination of correct statements is:
option_a: 2, 3 and 4 are correct
explanation: Workload is considered acceptable when it utilizes about 60% of the crew's cognitive resources, leaving a safety margin for unexpected events, and is heavily dependent on the pilot's expertise.

question_text: Motivation is a quality wich is often considered vital in the pilot's work to maintain safety.
option_a: However, excessive motivation leads to stress wich adversly affects performance
option_b: Motivation reduces the intensity of sensory illusions
option_c: A high degree of motivation makes it possible to make up for insufficient knowledge in complete safety
option_d: A high degree of motivation lowers the level of vigilance
explanation: While motivation is essential for safety and performance, excessive motivation can lead to high arousal and stress, which degrades cognitive performance and decision-making.

question_text: The quality of learning :
option_a: is promoted by feedback on the value of one's own performance
option_c: is independent of the level of motivation
explanation: The effectiveness of the learning process is highly promoted by receiving accurate, timely feedback regarding the quality of one's own performance.

question_text: Mental training, mental rehearsal of cognitive pretraining is called the inner, ideomotor simulation of actions.
option_a: It is most important for the acquisition of complex perceptual motor skills
option_b: It is most important for selfcontrol
option_c: It is most effective, if it is practiced on an abstract level if imagination
option_d: It is more effective than training by doing
explanation: Mental rehearsal (ideomotor training) involves mentally simulating actions and procedures, which is highly effective for acquiring and refining complex motor and flying skills.

question_text: How can the process of learning be facilitated?
option_a: By reinforcing successful trials
option_b: By increasing the psychological pressure on the student
option_c: By punishing the learner for unsuccessful trials
explanation: The learning process is facilitated by reinforcing successful trials, which strengthens the correct neural pathways and behaviors, whereas punishment is counterproductive.

question_text: Learning is called each lasting change of behaviour due to
option_a: practice and experience
explanation: Learning is defined as a relatively permanent change in behavior or capability resulting from practice and experience, as opposed to changes from maturation or drug influences.

question_text: Mental training is helpful to improve flying skills
option_a: at all levels of flying proficiency
option_d: only at a certain level of flying experience
explanation: Mental training and rehearsal are beneficial for improving cognitive and manual flying skills at all levels of pilot experience, from novices to flight instructors.

question_text: Which of the following are primary sources of motivation in day-to-day professional life ?1. Beeing in control of one's own situation2. Fear of punishment3. Success (achievement of goals)4. Social promotion, money
explanation: Primary sources of motivation in professional aviation include having control over one's situation, fear of negative outcomes, achieving personal and flight goals, and social status/financial compensation.

question_text: Which of the following statements summarises the impact that motivation may have on attention ?
option_a: It increases the mobilisation of energy and thus facilitates the quality of alertness and attention
option_b: It only facilitates attention in extreme cases (risk of death)
option_c: Motivation has only a small effect on attention, but it facilitates alertness
option_d: It stimulates attention but may lead to phases of low arousal
explanation: Motivation increases the mobilization of physiological energy, which enhances alertness, vigilance, and the quality of attention during demanding tasks.

question_text: The effect of experience and habit on performance
option_a: can both be beneficial and negative
explanation: Experience and habit are highly beneficial because they automate tasks and reduce cognitive workload, but they can also be negative by causing complacency and routine slips.

question_text: Murphy's law states :
option_a: If equipment is designed in such a way that it can be operated wrongly, then sooner or later, it will be
option_b: Response to a particular stressful influence varies from one person to another
option_c: Expectation has an influence on perception
explanation: Murphy's law is a design principle stating that if a system or piece of equipment can be operated incorrectly, it eventually will be, highlighting the need for error-tolerant designs.

question_text: The needs of an individual lead to :
option_a: a change in the individuals motivation and consequently to an adaptation of the behaviour
option_b: preservation from dangers only if social needs are beeing satisfied
option_c: no change in his motivation and conrequently to the persistence of the individuals behaviour in regard to the desired outcome
option_d: prolonged suppression of all basic needs in favour of high self-actualization
explanation: An individual's physiological and psychological needs shape their motivation, driving them to adapt their behavior to satisfy those needs and achieve desired safety outcomes.

question_text: Whilst flying a coordinated turn, most of your activity is
option_a: skill based behaviour
explanation: Flying a coordinated turn is a highly automated sensorimotor task for an experienced pilot, representing skill-based behavior in the SRK taxonomy.

question_text: If you approach an airfield VFR at a prescribed altitude, exactly following the approach procedure, and you encounter no inexpected or new problems you show:
option_a: skill based behaviour
explanation: Flying a standard VFR approach exactly according to procedures under normal conditions requires skill-based behavior for manual control and rule-based behavior for procedure compliance.

question_text: The choice of the moment you select flaps depending on situation and conditions of the landing is:
option_a: skill based behaviour
explanation: Configuring the aircraft, such as selecting when to extend flaps during an approach, is a routine motor sequence that represents skill-based behavior for an experienced pilot.

question_text: The readiness for tracing information which could indicate the development of a critical situation
option_a: is necessary to maintain good situational awareness
option_b: is dangerous, because it distracts attention from flying the aircraft
option_c: makes no sense because the human information processing system is limited anyway
option_d: is responsible for the development of inadequate mental models of the real world
explanation: To maintain high situational awareness, a pilot must remain actively vigilant and ready to detect any cues that could indicate the development of an abnormal or critical situation.

question_text: 1. Lively information is easier to take into consideration for creating a mental picture than boring information.2.The sequence in which information is offered is also important for the use the pilot makes of it.
option_a: 1 and 2 are both correct
explanation: Vivid, high-contrast information is easier for the brain to process into a mental model, and the sequence in which information is received significantly shapes how a pilot interprets it.

question_text: The development of procedures makes pilots more effective and more reliable in their actions. This is called:
option_a: procedural consistency
explanation: Standardizing operating procedures (SOPs) ensures that flight crew actions are consistent, predictable, and reliable, which helps prevent errors even under high-stress conditions.

question_text: What means can be used to combat human error?-1 : Reducing error-prone mechanisms.-2 : Improving the way in which error is taken into account in training.-3 : Sanctions against the initiators of error.-4 : Improving recovery from errors and its consequences.The combination of correct statements is:
option_a: 1, 2 and 4
explanation: To effectively manage and mitigate human error, safety systems must focus on reducing error-inducing designs, improving error management training, and enhancing error recovery.

question_text: It is desirable to standardize as many patterns of behaviour (operating procedures) as possible in commercial aviation mainly because
option_a: such behaviour reduces errors even under adverse circumstances
option_b: this lowers the ability requirement in pilot selection
option_c: this reduces the amount of training required
option_d: it makes the flight deck easier to design
explanation: Standardizing cockpit procedures in commercial aviation is critical because it ensures consistent crew behavior, which reduces slips and mistakes under adverse conditions.

question_text: Human errors are frequent and may take several forms :
option_a: an error can be described as the mismatch between the pilots intention and the result of his/her actions
option_b: an error of intention is an error of routine
option_c: an violation is an error which is always involuntary
option_d: representational errors in which the pilot has properly identified the situation and is familiar with the procedure
explanation: Human error is defined as a mismatch between a pilot's intention and the actual outcome of their actions, occurring in various forms like slips, lapses, and mistakes.

question_text: What is meant by the term 'complacency'?
option_a: Careless negligence or unjustified self-confidence
option_c: An agreement between captain and co-pilot due to Crew Resources Management
option_d: Physiological consequences on pilots because of fear of flying
explanation: Complacency is a dangerous psychological state in aviation characterized by careless negligence, self-satisfaction, and unjustified self-confidence, often leading to a lack of vigilance.

question_text: What would be the priority aim in the design of man-machine interfaces and in the creation of their application procedures for combatting problems associated with human error ?
option_a: To reduce the risks of the appearance or non-detection of errors entailing serious consequences
option_b: To eliminate the risk of latent errors occuring
option_c: To cater systematically for the consequences of errors in order to analyse their nature and modify ergonomic parameters
option_d: To put in place redundant alarm systems
explanation: The primary goal of cockpit interface and procedural design is to reduce the occurrence and prevent the non-detection of human errors that carry serious safety consequences.

question_text: How can man cope with low error tolerant situations?
option_a: By constantly complying with cross-over verification procedures (cross monitoring)
option_b: By increasing error detection in all circumstances
option_c: By randomly applying a combination of optimum detection, warning and monitoring systems
option_d: By generally avoiding situations in which tolerance to error is low
explanation: To manage safety in low error-tolerant situations, flight crews must strictly adhere to cross-monitoring, challenge-and-response checklists, and mutual verification procedures.

question_text: What are the various means which allow for better error detection?-1 : Improvement of the man-machine interface.-2 : Development of systems for checking the consistency of situations.-3 : Compliance with cross-over redundant procedures by the crew.-4 : Adaptation of visual alarms to all systems.The correct statement(s) is (are):
option_a: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Effective error detection in the cockpit relies on user-friendly interface designs, automatic system consistency checks, and crew compliance with redundant cross-checking procedures.

question_text: Why must flight safety considerations consider the human error mechanism? -1 : It is analysis of an incident or accident which will make it possible to identify what error has been committed and by whom. It is the process whereby the perpetrator is made responsible which may lead to elimination of the error.-2 : If we have a better understanding of the cognitive error mechanism, it will be possible to adapt procedures, aircraft interfaces, etc. -3 : It is error management procedure which enables us to continuously adjust our actions. The better we understand the underlying mechanism of an error, the better will be our means for detecting and adapting future errors.-4 : Since error is essentially human, once it has been identified by the use of procedures, a person will be able to anticipate and deal with it automatically in the future.The correct statement(s) is (are):
option_a: 2 and 3
explanation: Flight safety must study human error because understanding the cognitive mechanisms of errors allows designers to adapt procedures and cockpit interfaces to prevent future occurrences.

question_text: Improvement of human reliability should entail:
option_a: an effort to understand the causes and find means of recovery for errors committed
option_b: in aviation, the elimination of errors on the part of front-line operators
option_c: the elimination of latent errors before they can effect performance
option_d: the analysis of modes of human failures
explanation: Improving human reliability in the cockpit requires analyzing and understanding the underlying causes of errors to develop effective recovery and mitigation strategies.

question_text: An excessive need for safety
option_a: hampers severly the way of pilot decision making
option_b: is absolute necessary for a safe flight operation
option_c: is the most important attribute of a line pilot
option_d: guarantees the right decision making in critical situations
explanation: An excessive, pathological need for absolute safety can lead to hesitation, analysis paralysis, and a severe impairment of the pilot's decision-making ability in dynamic situations.

question_text: Studies of human error rates during the performance of simple repetitive task have shown, that errors can normally be expected to occur about
option_a: 1 in 10 times
explanation: Research shows that during simple, repetitive tasks without checking procedures, humans naturally commit errors at a rate of approximately 1 in 10 times.

question_text: Which of the following human error rates can be described as both realistic and pretty good, after methodical training
option_a: 1 in 100 times
explanation: Following methodical training and utilizing checklists, the human error rate for routine tasks can be stabilized at a highly reliable level of approximately 1 in 100 times.

question_text: Situations particularly vulnerable to ""reversion to an earlier behaviour pattern"" are :1. when concentration on a particular task is relaxed2. when situations are characterised by medium workload3. when situations are characterised by stress
option_a: 1. and 3.
explanation: A pilot is highly vulnerable to reverting to earlier, obsolete behavior patterns (such as operating controls from a previous aircraft type) when under stress or when attention is relaxed.

question_text: The most dangerous characteristic of the false mental model is, that it
option_a: is frequently extremely resistant to correction
option_b: will mainly occur under conditions of relaxation
option_c: will only occur under conditions of stress
explanation: The most dangerous characteristic of a false mental model is that it is highly resistant to correction, as confirmation bias causes the pilot to reject or ignore contradictory evidence.

question_text: Which of the following statements best fits the definition of an active error?Active error is:
option_a: produced by the operator and can be rapidly detected via the effects and consequences which it induces on the overall action
option_b: produced either by a front-line operator or by a remote operator and results in a hidden or latent consequence at a specific moment of the action
option_c: essentially results from the application of a bad rule or the poor application of a good rule by airplane designers
option_d: rare in front-line actions and difficult to detect owing to the fact that it usually occurs in a complex system of uncontrolled and involuntary deviations
explanation: An active error is an unsafe act committed by a front-line operator (such as a pilot) that has immediate, visible consequences on the safety of the flight.

question_text: What are the main consequences of latent errors?
